#3460. Why Batman: The Animated Series Chose Man-Bat As Its First Villain

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Batman: The Animated Series" is darker than most superhero cartoons before and since — literally darker. Drawn on black paper, "Batman: The Animated Series" presents Gotham City like an art deco painting mixed with an old Hollywood crime movie. But it wasn't only gangsters that went bump in the night. The very first episode, "On Leather Wings," uses one of the most out-there Batman villains: Man-Bat, aka zoologist Kirk Langstrom (Marc Singer), transformed by a potion into a half-man/half-bat creature like a winged werewolf.

Debuting in 1970's "Detective Comics" #400 by Frank Robbins and Neal Adams, Man-Bat had 20+ years of comics history behind him when "On Leather Wings" was made. But for non-comic fans, that episode would be the first time they'd seen him. According to "Batman: The Animated Series" co-creator Bruce Timm, that's exactly why he was the pilot's villain. In "Modern Masters Volume 3: Bruce Timm," he recounted:

"Man-Bat was chosen specifically [for the first episode] because he wasn't familiar to very many people outside of comic book fans. Nobody had any preconceived notions about him. It wasn't like the Joker, where you had to deal with people expecting him to be Jack Nicholson or Cesar Romero."

"On Leather Wings" was written by Mitch Brian, who had also developed the "Batman" series bible. What became "On Leather Wings" originated as an episode premise in that bible, though with the gruesome detail that Man-Bat was killing tourists, which isn't in the episode as made. Brian has said he pushed for Man-Bat to give the series a dash of the fantastical right off the bat (no pun intended) — "Batman: The Animated Series" could do not just film noir, but also Universal Horror-esque mad science and monsters.

Man-Bat as Batman's first villain also carries narrative symmetry. His moniker is a twist on Batman's own and he takes Batman's mission to "become a bat" one step further. "Man-Bat kind of works because he's literally the reverse of Batman and he's also got the obsessive interest in bats," said Bruce Timm in "Modern Masters."

Now, technically, Catwoman's debut episode "The Cat and the Claw" premiered first on September 5, 1992, one day earlier than "On Leather Wings" did. "Batman Returns," starring Michelle Pfeiffer as Catwoman, had hit theaters that past summer. (Currently, "The Cat and the Claw" is also listed as the first episode of "Batman: The Animated Series" on HBO Max.) But, functionally, "On Leather Wings" is a much better pilot episode — because that's what it was made to be.

It also demonstrated that "Batman: The Animated Series" was more than just a movie tie-in, down to the choice of villain. In "I Am The Night: The Ultimate Unauthorized History of Batman Series," author Daniel Dockery notes a villain like Man-Bat would've been "nigh impossible to pull off in live-action." Remember, this was 1992, a year before "Jurassic Park" unlocked the potential of CGI. A human-sized bat monster? And an action scene where it flies through Gotham with Batman towed behind it on a rope? Yeah, in the 1990s, a live-action "Batman" movie that even attempted any of that would look ridiculous. But in a cartoon, it was thrilling, and proved "Batman: The Animated Series" was a canvas for unique Batman stories.

Starting with "On Leather Wings" also highlights another tenet from the aforementioned "Batman" series bible: no origin story episodes, because the audience already knew Batman's origin from decades of prior "Batman" comics, movies, and cartoons.

During "On Leather Wings," the police mistake Man-Bat for Batman (Kevin Conroy) and hunt the Dark Knight instead. This premise rests on Gotham City already knowing Batman, which is only possible because the series starts in media res with Batman as an experienced crimefighter. The first time we see Batman is deliberately unspectacular; he's sitting in the Batcave, in costume, reading a newspaper article about the Man-Bat attacks.

The "Batman is framed" subplot also demonstrates that this isn't the Adam West show where Batman is literally deputized by the police and trusted by all of Gotham as a paragon of justice. Many people are already scared of Batman, so it's not a huge leap to blame him for Man-Bat's attacks. (The series' movie spin-off, "Batman: Mask of the Phantasm," even used a nigh-identical story, with Batman being mistaken for the film's eponymous villain.)

Turning Man-Bat's identity into a mystery differs from his first appearance in the comics. There, we meet Man-Bat as Langstrom first and see his gradual and tragic transformation. Mitch Brian compared Man-Bat to "The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde," and by making "On Leather Wings" a mystery, it brings Man-Bat closer to that book. It also, crucially, allows Batman to act as a detective. The twist of Man-Bat being Langstrom works because, again, he's not a villain most of the audience already knew inside-and-out.

Artist Kevin Nowlan, who had drawn a Man-Bat story in DC's "Secret Origins" #39, was initially recruited to design the villain. (See his concept art above.) Bruce Timm's finalized design includes his characters' standard broad upper chest, which fits well with Man-Bat's arms growing out into wings. In form and function, Man-Bat was the perfect pilot villain for "Batman: The Animated Series."

Wicker might not get any Oscar recognition (although that would be a pleasant surprise), but I'd argue it's one of the best theater-going experiences of any film released on the 2026 movie schedule. Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård’s unconventional rom-com turned out to be much more than a smutty romance about a perfect man built of wicker. Audiences were won over not only by Skarsgård’s wicker abs, but also his character’s pure heart, leaving many hungry for more, Skarsgård included. And I laughed out loud when I heard the “sequel” he’s been pitching.

Alexander Skarsgård has never been one to take himself too seriously, especially while doing press tours. I can’t say I blame him, doing the same interviews over and over would get pretty old otherwise. However, his effortless deadpan and jesting tendencies make it difficult to sometimes tell if he’s being serious or not, like with this recent pitch to Entertainment Weekly about a Wicker follow-up:

It’s called Corduroy. We tried to find financing for it, but, for some reason, it’s been hard, but we’re pitching it around Hollywood this week.

At this point, I can’t tell if this is a serious pitch or not, but the idea is genuinely hilarious. Skarsgård added that this corduroy character would be “delicate and soft,” as well as an “attentive lover.” I’ve got to be honest, that doesn’t sound as sexy as a sturdily built wicker man, but I get the sense this concept is in very early stages of development. Forget splinters, we’d be wondering about carpet burn.

Seriously, I’m going to need someone to ask the A-lister about this again, because I really need some clarification. Skarsgård is known to joke with the media, even tot he point of teasing a “smear” campaign against his father, Stellan Skarsgård (Sentimental Value) during awards season. However, I wouldn’t put it past him to actually try and get this wild sequel made.

I’m just not fully sold on “Corduroy” for another reason. If your mind went to the same place as mine upon hearing this pitch, you understand why. Yes, I’m talking about the children’s story “Corduroy,” in which a corduroy teddy bear comes to life in a department store. Given Wicker’s salacious content and marketing, it feels really weird to relate the two, and therefore I fear it might be difficult to get that sequel pitch off the ground. However, the Legend of Tarzan actor has been persistent in the idea of a Wicker sequel, and I’m curious to see what that might look like.

This isn’t the first time the Northman actor has pitched a sequel to his latest movie. During the press tour, Skarsgård expressed interest in continuing the Wicker Husband’s story, following questions about what happens at the end of Wicker when the unconventional family of three leaves their village behind.

Clearly, Skarsgård enjoyed playing the wicker sex symbol that has taken the internet by storm, but that’s not surprising. If 2025’s kinky Pillion taught us anything, it’s that Skarsgård isn’t afraid to get a lil freaky (in the best ways) and Wicker seems to have opened a whole new realm of possibilities in his mind.

However, between the wicker husband’s kind heart and the fairytale-like setting that allows this somewhat raunchy, yet overall heartwarming love story to take place, I’m just not sure the same effect would work with a “corduroy husband” or any other textile husband for that matter. I’ll be quite surprised if something along these lines pops up on the 2027 movie schedule, but you can bet I’ll still buy a ticket. In the meantime, check out Wicker in theaters now.

#3457. Mads Mikkelsen Delivered His Best Performance In This Unforgettable 2012 Movie

Few European actors have found the blend of native and international success that Mads Mikkelsen has. Born in Denmark, he became a star in his home country during the 1990s and 2000s, his career kicking off with Nicolas Winding Refn's 1996 crime thriller "Pusher." He's since become a favorite of Hollywood productions, too, starting with his role as the Bond villain Le Chiffre in "Casino Royale."

Since then, Mikkelsen has remained a go-to Hollywood bad guy, appearing in blockbusters like Marvel Studios' "Doctor Strange." He's also one of the privileged few to have played arguably the most famous screen villain ever, Hannibal Lecter. More than a few would argue Mikkelsen's Lecter in the 2013 TV series "Hannibal" is even better than Anthony Hopkins in "The Silence of the Lambs."

Mikkelsen's razor-sharp cheekbones, intense stare, and European accent instantly code him as "villain" in Hollywood language. When "Rogue One: A Star Wars Story" cast him as Galen Erso, a sympathetic scientist conscripted into building the Death Star, it read as casting against type to American audiences. But look at Mikkelsen's Danish resume and you'll find he's a much more diverse actor than the box that Hollywood has stuck him inside. Amusingly, one of those movies — Thomas Vinterberg's "The Hunt" — stars Mikkelsen as a good man mistakenly persecuted as a villain.

Lucas (Mikkelsen) is a Danish kindergarten teacher. One of his students, his best friend Theo's (Thomas Bo Larsen) daughter Klara (Annika Wedderkopp), has a puppy love crush on him. Obviously, he gently turns her down. Klara then vengefully suggests to the school principal that Lucas exposed himself to or molested her. (In reality, as the movie shows, her crude older brother shoved an iPad displaying porn in her face.) The ugly rumor grows out of control, and Lucas' reputation pays the price.

In "The Hunt," the town rushes to the worst possible conclusion about Lucas. All but a few loved ones like his son, Marcus (Lasse Fogelstrøm), believe the worst from hearsay. But they don't actually know it for a fact (indeed, what ultimately helps clear Lucas is the facts pointing in his favor). The movie is never ambiguous, though; we know from the very beginning that Lucas is innocent and this is all just a terrible tragedy of miscommunication. "The Hunt" also avoids reactionary narratives about scorned women peddling false rape allegations because Klara is a young child. She simply doesn't grasp the consequences of what she did, as is the case with the other preschoolers who echo her claims.

Compare a similar recent film, "Fjord," inspired by a real-life story about a Norwegian evangelical couple whose children were taken from them after suspicions of abuse. Like in "The Hunt," the allegations are implied to stem from leading questions and miscommunication from the kids. But "Fjord" counterintuitively stacks the deck in the parents' favor while trying to present objectivity, perhaps because it knows many left-leaning audiences are inclined to side against the conservative couple and takes perverse enjoyment in testing those sympathies.

A film like "The Hunt" could choose not to reveal Lucas' innocence either way or cast doubt, inviting you to sympathize with a possible monster as an endurance test. But the reality of "The Hunt," seeing an innocent man be branded with a scarlet letter, is also agonizing to watch in its own way. It's a modern iteration on the parable of the feathers in the wind, and how once spoken, even untruthful gossip can't be erased.

As Lucas, Mikkelsen sheds any of the power or menace he projects as a villain in those aforementioned Hollywood movies. "The Hunt" is also a Danish-language film, and Mikkelsen's comfort with his native tongue also makes for an even more seamless performance.

To this day, I've never forgotten the catharsis of a scene where Lucas stands up for himself. After being assaulted in a grocery store, he walks in again, headbutts the hostile clerk, and demands his groceries back. The first time I watched "The Hunt," I rewound the movie to see the scene a second time.

That relatively late-in-the-movie scene is a well-earned respite from Lucas' victimhood. Even in a story like this, too much passivity from a protagonist turns into a chore. Lucas similarly takes matters into his own hands at the movie's emotional climax. Again, Klara's father Theo is Lucas' best friend; while Theo takes Klara's side, he claims to know Lucas so well he can tell when he's lying or truthful by just looking into his eyes. Lucas goes to Christmas Mass, putting himself dead center in the community that has exiled him, and looks at Theo across the pews.

The power of this lynchpin scene is in Mikkelsen's silent, icy stare (Lucas pointedly ditches his glasses during this scene). But it's not the aloof stare of Le Chiffre or the predatory one of Hannibal Lecter. In his sad eyes and slight frown, Lucas is begging Theo to read the truth on his face. When that's not enough, he storms over to Theo, sobbing, and refuses to let him look away from his eyes.

Mads Mikkelsen is an extraordinary actor, and yet the greatest proof of that is him playing a normal man in "The Hunt."

A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus. Bose positions it right in the middle of the SoundLink lineup, and you feel that balance in how it’s built. #3455. 9 Giant-Sized Changes Marvel Made to Ant-Man After Edgar Wright Left

Unsurprisingly, that Falcon cameo would not have been in there

In May 2014, it was announced that Edgar Wright, best known for movies like Shaun of the Dead and Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, would no longer be directing Marvel’s Ant-Man movie. The news was shocking because Wright was not just a director-for-hire like some Marvel filmmakers have been. Wright first began crafting his Ant-Man film with co-writer Joe Cornish in the early 2000s, before the Marvel Cinematic Universe was even a thing. When the MCU began to develop, Wright’s Ant-Man was one of the earliest confirmed projects. Wright was even a part of the MCU’s first panel back in 2006.

As Wright has explained in interviews, he was excited to be on the ground floor of something, setting the tone for what the MCU would become. He wanted to do a superhero movie where it was still emblematic of the director, in keeping with their body of work. The comparison he’d made was Tim Burton’s Batman, which is still very much a Tim Burton movie. After leaving Ant-Man, Wright even told Variety, “I wanted to make a Marvel movie but I don’t think they really wanted to make an Edgar Wright movie.”

Part of the problem was timing. Ant-Man was originally a Phase One MCU movie, with only loose connective tissue to the other films. But Wright asked that Ant-Man be pushed back so that he could direct The World’s End first. This was because his producing partner, Eric Fellner, had been diagnosed with cancer and he wanted to finish their “Cornetto Trilogy” while Fellner still could.

Marvel agreed and Ant-Man moved to Phase Two, after the blockbuster success of Avengers and when Marvel’s “house style” had already been established. As Wright and Cornish were updating their drafts of the film and casting the major parts, Marvel kept pushing for more connections with the MCU. Eventually, Marvel had one of its in-house screenwriters do a draft without Wright’s involvement. This eventually resulted in Wright's departure, and director Peyton Reed took his place. Paul Rudd, who was already cast as Scott Lang, then did a rewrite with Adam McKay, which became the film we now know.

To be clear, a good amount of Wright and Cornish’s script survived and served as the film’s overall backbone. According to Reed, “The idea to make Ant-Man a heist movie structure was all Edgar and Joe. The idea of Hank Pym and Scott Lang as mentor and pupil, again, that was all theirs, and also, the idea of a movie that that all drives toward a third act where the big battle between the good guy and the bad guy takes place in a little girl's bedroom, that was always there from the beginning, and I stand by the fact that I think that's genius.”

Still, there were a lot of changes, and while we’ve never seen the original script (and Wright has said he has to be careful about revealing too much because of the NDA he signed) there’s enough out there to give us a pretty good idea of the differences. Here are the nine biggest changes from Edgar Wright's Ant-Man to the one we got.

In the version of Ant-Man that we got, Scott Lang’s crew for pulling off heists was just three guys, but according to the film’s editor Colby Parker Jr., “I think there were, like, 15 people within the gang.”

Michael Peña’s character Luis did exist in Wright’s version, but in a much smaller capacity, most likely because Scott Lang’s crew would have been so much bigger. But as the movie took a new direction under Reed, his part grew and once they got into reshoots, his character grew even more. Even that famous summary montage Luis did was a late addition.

This one probably isn't a big surprise, as Falcon's fight with Ant-Man definitely feels shoehorned into the movie. Wright’s version had far less crossover with the existing MCU. As Parker Jr. told The Direct, "I don't think there would have been any other Marvel characters set up. I think he was going to be a standalone. He didn't want any other Marvel characters in the film.” Parker Jr. even specifically pointed to the scene, saying, “I don't think the Falcon would have been in Ant-Man.

According to the book MCU: The Reign of Marvel Studios, Edgar Wright’s Ant-Man would have begun with a flashback to Hank Pym (Michael Douglas) as the original Ant-Man, then it would have jumped to the present day with Scott Lang stealing the suit.

With Wright opening on Pym as Ant-Man, the movie would not have featured the scene with Hank Pym fighting with Peggy Carter and Howard Stark about trying to replicate his Pym Particles.

As Peyton Reed told Vulture, “In the original drafts I think there was one reference in dialogue to Janet. She didn’t appear in the movie.” While Janet Van Dyne — who would eventually come to be played by Michelle Pfeiffer in Ant-Man and the Wasp — only appears briefly in Ant-Man, her absence informs much of Hank Pym’s arc with his daughter Hope (Evangeline Lilly) and builds into the Quantum Realm story for the sequel. Speaking of which…

“We also brought the quantum realm into the movie, which was never in the early drafts,” Reed told Vulture. “That mostly came about because Adam and I love that psychedelic part of Marvel Comics. We thought, ‘There’s gonna be a lot of shrinking in this movie. What if we got to the third act and we took it even further?’ We found a way to work that into the story with the self-sacrifice that Scott makes to save his daughter, but it also leaves Hank Pym with this realization that Scott got out of the quantum realm, something he didn’t think was possible.”

Considering how important the quantum realm is to the MCU, especially for Avengers: Endgame, it’s clear that Wright’s departure didn’t just change Ant-Man, it changed the entire MCU.

In the final version of Ant-Man, Scott Lang is an ex-con in the very loosest sense, having committed some anti-corporate crime where he did some Robin Hood kind of thing, stealing corporate money and giving it to people who had been scammed by the company. But in Wright’s version, Lang started out as an “actual criminal,” Wright explained on his Instagram, with a greater redemption arc throughout the film. This undoubtedly would have changed the character, and probably would have made him a bit more interesting.

Evangeline Lilly, who came onto the film as Hope Van Dyne because of Edgar Wright, was a big supporter of his and almost left the film in solidarity. Eventually, she was convinced to stay on and, after having seen the finished film directed by Reed, she told The Hollywood Reporter that Wright's version “wouldn’t have fit in the Marvel Universe. It would have stuck out like a sore thumb, no matter how good it was. It just would have taken you away from this cohesive universe they’re trying to create.”

#3454. Is The Rings Of Power Connected To Peter Jackson's Lord Of The Rings Trilogy?

The canon of the "Lord of the Rings" movie and TV franchise has become a little complicated in recent years. Sauron's war finally arrives in "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, and with the show's return, it's worth asking: Is this series canonical to Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" films? We finally have a firm answer, and it's ... sort of (if we read between the lines).

In a recent interview with Screen Rant, "The Rings of Power" co-showrunner Patrick McKay addressed the canon question head-on without giving a simple "yes" or "no" answer. Still he made it pretty clear where things stand, explaining, "There is room in Middle-earth for everybody, and we're fans of those films, and we hope it's great." (He was referring to the already controversial upcoming film "The Hunt for Gollum" with that last bit.)

In terms of the "Lord of the Rings" timeline, "The Rings of Power" is set thousands of years before the "Lord of the Rings" movies. So, in theory, they could work together. Speaking further though, McKay established that the show exists alongside the many interpretations of J.R.R. Tolkien's Middle-earth books over the years and not necessarily as part of any other adaptation (including Jackson's):

"So many talented artists in so many mediums over 75 years have interpreted this material, painted or drawn it, or put it in a song or made it into a film or an animated film. I think to sit on a shelf with all those other works, we are only too delighted for that to be our fate."

He added that the movies and the show are "in conversation with one another." Put simply, then, "The Rings of Power" is not strictly canon within the universe of Jackson's films.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" brings the fabled Second Age of Middle-earth's history to life on-screen for the first time. Therefore, it's centuries removed from both the events of J.R.R. Tolkien's "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings" books and Peter Jackson's film adaptations alike.

Even so, it initially looked like Jackson was going to be involved with "The Rings of Power," only for Amazon to ghost him while developing the Prime Video series. Why? In essence, it was apparently a contractual matter. In a statement issued in 2022, Amazon claimed, "In pursuing the rights for our show, we were obligated to keep the series distinct and separate from the films." So, basically, "The Rings of Power" can't, for legal reasons, be officially canonical to Jackson's movies. Of course, Patrick McKay couldn't just come out and say that, so he found a more diplomatic way to go about it.

Jackson, obviously, is the man that turned "The Lord of the Rings" into the one fantasy franchise to rule them all, as his adaptations of J.R.R. Tolkien's books became massive, beloved hits that have endured for decades. Still, while it makes sense that Amazon would, in theory, want him to work on "The Rings of Power," it seems securing the rights for the show meant sacrifices had to be made.

Nevertheless, Jackson is producing (but not directing) "The Hunt for Gollum," with Gollum actor Andy Serkis helming the movie himself. Warner Bros. is also developing another "LOTR" movie co-written by superfan Stephen Colbert, so this franchise has a future on the big screen as well.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" is streaming now on Prime Video.

At the very start of Dancing with the Stars' 35th season, I thought Harry Shum Jr. was the ultimate frontrunner. However, I quickly came to love Ezra Frech. His story is remarkable and empowering. Plus, he’s so naturally talented, and he's partnered with one of my favorite pros, Daniella Karagach. So, as the weeks have passed on the 2026 TV schedule, I’ve wanted him to win. However, as each episode has gone by and that appreciation for Frech has stayed consistent, my love for Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov just keeps growing stronger and stronger.

While I always thought Amber was one to watch, she’s proven time and time again that she and her partner are helping set the gold standard for this season. Then, the figure skater went on the Zach Sang Show to talk about her experience on DWTS, and she said something about winning that really made her the frontrunner in my mind. When asked what it’d mean to get Pasha his first mirrorball, the Olympian said:

That would mean the world, because, I’ve said this before, is that I came into this competition, of course, who doesn’t want to win. But it wasn’t like, ‘I need this because I’ve worked my entire life for it.’ Like, I’ve been dancing for two months. Yes, it has been a very intense, very passionate two months of working, but it has been his whole life that he has been dancing. And he’s been on the show for, I believe, nine seasons. And every single year, he has put his everything into every single celeb he’s had.

Pasha has been on the show for eight seasons, and with each year, I love him and his wife, Daniella, even more. Seriously, season after season, I find myself more invested in the pros than the stars. That’s because they’re there year after year, and I get to know them all quite well through the show and social media. So, while I adore them all, and my love for Daniella is very strong, I have wanted Pasha to get his flowers really, really badly.

In his eight seasons, the highest place he’s ever gotten is third, and he deserves a win. Amber is the perfect person to help him do it. As she explained, he wanted to have an athlete as a partner, and she has “the stamina and the physical capabilities” to do tougher dances. She also complimented her partner’s ability to teach, and ended up saying:

There’s no reason that we shouldn’t be able to make this happen besides me limiting myself.

Her drive to do this for her partner is so endearing, and it’s now a big reason why I want her to win. Along with that, the Olympian went on to detail how much work the pros have to do for this show. While it looks hard for the stars, the pros have to do twice as much, and she wants Pasha to get recognized for it, explaining:

He has been putting everything into this, and I really want for everyone to see him succeed. Because it is technically, you know, every year it’s the celeb, but it’s also about the pros. Like, he is putting – imagine how much work I’m putting into it; he’s doing twice the amount. He has to choreograph; he has to do so many visual selections. Like, there’s so much that the pro does for every single show that people don’t see. So, yes, it’s about the celebrity and who wins, but it is also about the pro.

Of course, all the pros have to do this, and I'm sure their stars would praise them the same way Amber praised Pasha. However, her passion is infectious, and that, paired with their fun and high-quality dances, makes them my No. 1 couple.

Plus, of the vets still on the show who have been there for over seven seasons, Mark Ballas, Jenna Johnson, and Daniella have won before; Pasha has not.

So, yes, while I’ll be happy if Ezra and Daniella win, because they are amazing, right now, I’m rooting harder for Amber and Pasha. They are killing it week after week, and Amber’s drive to win for her pro and get him his first mirrorball is making me even more motivated to text “Amber” to 21523 as many times as I possibly can.

Now, to see who takes home the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, make sure to tune in to the last few weeks of Dancing with the Stars on Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET either on ABC or with a Disney+ subscription.

#3452. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3451. 15 Best Hard Sci-Fi Movies Of All Time, Ranked

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

While science fiction includes everything from space opera to cyberpunk, one sub-genre that we have a special place for is hard sci-fi. These movies place a stronger emphasis on scientific accuracy and a more grounded premise than their more fantastical counterparts. Many of the best sci-fi movies ever are set within the realm of hard sci-fi, heightening the sense of realism to their stories. We're taking a closer look at this fan-favorite sub-genre and our personal favorite movies within it.

While there are varying opinions about what qualifies as hard sci-fi, each of the movies we're including here certainly have a strong scientific grounding. Even some of the best sci-fi movies of 2026 are clear hard sci-fi projects, breathing new life into the sub-genre. With those qualities in mind, these are the best 15 hard sci-fi movies of all time ranked, each offering their own cinematic verisimilitude to the genre.

After "2001: A Space Odyssey," there was "Marooned," with Gregory Peck's space thriller based on the novel of the same name by Martin Caidin. Peck stars as NASA Director Charles Keith who finds himself working on a desperate rescue mission to save three astronauts stranded in orbit. As the incident becomes more public, Keith is forced to use an experimental spacecraft for the rescue, despite it being untested. Meanwhile, the stranded astronauts grow desperate as they begin to run out of oxygen before help arrives.

"Marooned" was released before the Apollo 13 incident, which similarly saw American astronauts seemingly stranded in space. While things like the movie's experimental spacecraft take it to sci-fi territory, the whole thing feels scientifically plausible. At the same time, the movie also keeps a tight focus on the human stakes, including the response back home and the families affected by the incident. Overlooked by audiences today, nearly 60 years later, "Marooned" sets the template for so many subsequent space disaster movies on this list.

A big factor in a lot of hard sci-fi movies is its production budget, because it's far cheaper to make a grounded sci-fi movie than an outlandishly audacious one. That certainly informs the 2004 indie movie "Primer," written, directed, produced, edited, and starring Shane Carruth, who also composed the score. Carruth plays Aaron, an engineer whose colleague Abe (David Sullivan) develops an amateur time machine in their garage. As the duo explore the possibilities of their invention, they progressively experience the dire consequences of time travel.

While "Primer" may look and feel like a lofi time travel movie at first glance, it refreshingly explores its conflict from a well-thought approach. Things like the process' physical toll on the body from its wider ripple effects are smartly explored throughout the story. The production's DIY nature actually suits the narrative well, given the amateur nature of the movie's central plot device. If you haven't seen "Primer" before, the movie is a must-watch for sci-fi movie fans and a tightly constructed one at that.

1997's "Gattaca" is another sci-fi flick that feels eerily plausible for modern society to follow within the next several years. The story is set in a world where eugenics has become widespread to avoid the birth of babies with debilitating genetic conditions. This leads to society discriminating against those who carry genetic defects, including protagonist Vincent Freeman (Ethan Hawke). Posing as a genetically engineered individual, Vincent's ruse comes under scrutiny in the wake of a corporate executive's murder.

Admittedly, "Gattaca" is the most visually stylish movie on this list, but its concept and the level of technology depicted hold a real world weight to them. The science behind the story's genetic engineering and eugenics feels particularly well-developed as the cornerstone of this dystopian society. The movie goes into meticulous detail how Vincent is able to maintain his deception and how this genetic technology has impacted civilization. A dystopian noir look at the perils of artificial perfection, "Gattaca" is a moody flick that makes the most of its premise.

Filmmaker James Cameron's most underrated movie is the 1989 underwater thriller "The Abyss," with its core themes carried over into "Avatar: The Way of Water." The movie has American and Soviet teams racing to salvage a sunken American submarine from the bottom of the ocean. Leading the American expedition is an oil drilling crew headed by Bud Brigman (Ed Harris), only to find otherworldly entities are involved. As the full scope of this mission becomes apparent, Bud tries to stop hostilities from escalating between humanity and this underwater species.

More than just standing as another Cameron project that heavily involves the water, "The Abyss" also showcases his sharp attention to detail. Cameron takes care to demonstrate the real-world dangers of deep-sea exploration, including the high pressure and chilling temperatures of the watery depths. These elements fuel the tension as much as the strange creatures that Bud encounters, along with Cameron's recurring message that unchecked human aggression is the true enemy. Claustrophobically staged and under-appreciated for years, "The Abyss" is Cameron's unsung classic and as grounded his sci-fi work gets.

The first novel that author Michael Crichton published under his own name was 1969's "The Andromeda Strain," which was adapted for the silver screen in 1971. More intelligently assembled than the standard disaster movie fare of its time, the movie opens with a satellite crashing near a small town in New Mexico. After most of the community dies suddenly under mysterious causes, it's discovered that the satellite brought back a highly lethal extraterrestrial microorganism. The movie follows a team of scientists trying to contain the situation before it can wipe out all life on the planet.

Crichton's work tends to succeed the more firmly that they're rooted in reality before expanding into the fantastical. "The Andromeda Strain" is a prime example of this, still packing a punch over 50 years since its debut. That strong scientific approach to the premise underscores the gravity that this threat is terrifyingly plausible. Still one of the best Michael Crichton movie adaptations, "The Andromeda Strain" offers a grounded sci-fi approach to annihilation by contagion.

While the 1972 adaptation of "Solaris" by Soviet filmmaker Andrei Tarkovsky is one of the best space horror movies ever made, it does veer tonally away from Stanisław Lem's novel. By contrast, Steven Soderbergh's 2002 adaptation is more of a drama and an isolated character study, though some existential thriller elements remain. The movie's protagonist is Chris Kelvin (George Clooney), a clinical psychologist who visits a remote space station only to find most of its crew is dead. As Kelvin investigates the situation, he is shocked to be reunited with his late wife Rheya (Natascha McElhone). who is seemingly alive and well.

While it's a close call, Soderbergh's "Solaris" is a sci-fi remake that's better than the original, mostly because of change in tone and Clooney's vulnerable performance. This elevates the movie's ambiguous existential contemplation, while Soderbergh wisely keeps the sci-fi elements relatively stripped down. At its core, the story is a meditation on grief and guilt while Soderbergh builds his story in a relatively grounded outer space setting. Soderbergh's "Solaris" is both his most understated and boldest project, using the mysteries of the cosmos to explore its emotional themes.

The debut feature directorial project by British filmmaker Duncan Jones is the 2009 indie flick "Moon." The movie is largely a one-man show for Sam Rockwell, who plays Samuel Bell, a technician working alone in a lunar mining facility. As Bell nears the end of his three-year assignment, he begins to hallucinate, while his health steadily worsens. This culminates in Bell coming face-to-face with a doppelganger of himself, as he realizes the disturbing truth about his existence.

With its pragmatically minimalist art design and Rockwell being the only actor on-screen for the majority of the movie, "Moon" keeps its storytelling simple but effective. The idea that the Moon could be mined heavily for helium-3 is rooted in fact, while the technology is never particularly outlandish. Like Soderbergh's "Solaris," Jones keeps its narrative focus tightly on his protagonist which is where its real strength lies. An intimately scaled sci-fi thriller, "Moon" remains Duncan's best work to date, using its grounded backdrop to atmospheric effect.

Among the sci-fi movies that nobody talks about anymore is "Silent Running," which was released in 1972. The movie takes place in a future where Earth is no longer capable of supporting trees, forcing humanity to take its forestry off-world. The story is set in a spaceship serving as a large biome for trees, tended to meticulously by botanist Freeman Lowell (Bruce Dern). When the crew is ordered to destroy the biomes by their corporate overseers, Lowell goes through murderous lengths to defend his carefully curated forests.

Of all the movies on this list, "Silent Running" is the one with the most pointed sociopolitical commentary. From its takedown of corporate greed to its eco-friendly themes, the movie feels like both a product of its time and as prescient as ever. Dern is rarely better than in his performance as Lowell, with his character standing as a portrait of single-minded obsession and carrying much of the movie. Unabashedly direct in its messaging, "Silent Running" deserves wider recognition than it receives from the public these days.

Not every hard sci-fi movie needs to unfold in outer space or revolve around high concept narratives. The 2013 romantic drama "Her" is perfectly set within a more intimate scope, given its premise. Taking place in a near-future Los Angeles, loner Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) struggles at forming a meaningful romantic connection with others. Instead, Theodore grows closer to his digital assistant Samantha (Scarlett Johansson) as she gains sentience, with a loving relationship growing between them.

"Her" is the perfect love story for the Information Age, underscoring that technological advances don't necessarily separate us from connecting with others. The movie's premise feels entirely plausible while also being prescient in the decade prior to the widespread proliferation of artificial intelligence. The tightened focus works well, with filmmaker Spike Jonze keeping the "Her" set intimate for Joaquin Phoenix, as he stays awkwardly vulnerable for much of the story. Understated in its tone and scope but still packing an emotional wallop, "Her" is Jonze's humanist masterpiece in an increasingly digital era.

Among the most celebrated hard sci-fi authors of the 20th century was astronomer and science educator Carl Sagan. The 1997 movie "Contact" adapted Sagan's 1985 novel of the same name, detailing humanity's first contact with extraterrestrial life. After astronomer Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster) detects signs of intelligent otherworldly life, the world is galvanized by the discovery. Though Arroway wants to make contact with these mysterious figures through an experimental device, complications quickly arise.

While there is certainly extraterrestrial interaction to be had, "Contact" is more about the reaction and fallout to confirmation of otherworldly life. Jodie Foster brings that thoroughly human response to the subject matter, while her character guides audiences through the story. "Contact" could've been a much stranger movie, treating Sagan and partner Ann Druyan's tale with tone-deaf disregard for scientific accuracy and characterization, but cooler heads won out. One of the best sci-fi movies of the '90s, hard with its science or not, "Contact" is an understated genre gem.

Upon its debut in 2026, "Project Hail Mary" was quickly crowned as one of the best sci-fi movies ever and deservedly so. Based on the best-selling novel by Andy Weir, the movie has our sun plagued by a strange substance threatening to dim it to catastrophic levels within decades. Molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) is forced to join an interstellar expedition searching for a way to restore the sun's output. This leads Grace to team up with a rock-based extraterrestrial on his own mission to save his planet from the threat of the same substance.

"Project Hail Mary" improves upon Andy Weir's book in key ways, streamlining the story and quietly discarding its more superfluous sci-fi elements. But even with its interstellar partnership, the adaptation retains the source material's penchant for scientifically informed storytelling. That grounds the more cosmic elements as Grace finally enacts his last-ditch effort to save his world from chilly annihilation. Keeping hard sci-fi alive and well into the 2020s, "Project Hail Mary" is a bonafide crowd-pleaser.

Still one of Christopher Nolan's most ambitious movies over a decade after its release, "Interstellar" is the filmmaker's most high-flying tale to date. Like "Project Hail Mary" after it, the movie revolves around humanity at the brink of extinction, forced to undertake a desperate mission for its salvation. In the case of Nolan's story, Earth is rocked by severe dust storms affecting its agriculture, with astronaut Coop (Matthew McConaughey) leading an expedition for a habitable planet. This is juxtaposed by Coop's adult daughter Murph (Jessica Chastain) trying to find a way to create a spacecraft capable of launching into deep space through Earth's gravity.

While there are, of course, creative liberties taken through its premise, "Interstellar" boasts a high level of scientific accuracy. This includes the astrophysics propelling the story like the singularity that serves as the key to its spacefaring scope. Everything from planets undergoing significant time dilation to the gravity equation back on Earth all feel feasible, even with all the cinematic splendor. Christopher Nolan always offers a well-thought approach to even the most fantastical subject matter, and "Interstellar" captures those qualities beautifully.

Another British filmmaker who's excelled at smart sci-fi storytelling in the 21st century is Alex Garland. Arguably the hardest sci-fi story Garland has told thus far, and certainly one of the most effective, is the psychological thriller "Ex Machina." The story follows programmer Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) who stays at the remote home of eccentric tech CEO Nathan Bateman (Oscar Isaac). Caleb is tasked with checking the sentience of Bateman's latest creation, a self-aware android known as Ava (Alicia Vikander) only for things to violently go off the rails.

There is an underlying paranoia with existential overtones that permeate throughout "Ex Machina," carrying its narrative forward. Compared to more overtly cyberpunk stories like "Blade Runner," Garland's 2014 flick takes a much more grounded view on androids and the proliferation of artificial intelligence. This is underscored by its special effects, with the "Ex Machina" VFX avoiding green screen use, preferring practical effects and sets for its execution. A cautionary tale about billionaire vanity projects taking on a hostile life of their own, "Ex Machina" is Garland's most prescient work.

Another adaptation of an Andy Weir novel to mention here is 2015's "The Martian," directed and produced by Ridley Scott. The movie is set in a near-future where humanity has established a research station on Mars as part of an international coalition. After the station's team evacuates from the planet during a severe dust storm, astronaut Mark Watney (Matt Damon) is accidentally left behind. Until a rescue mission can be carried out, Watney has to rely on the tools that he has available and his own wits to survive alone on Mars.

Andy Weir gave the 2015 adaptation of "The Martian" his seal of approval, and we do too. The movie is Scott's most buoyantly light, yet it doesn't compromise the scientific know-how behind Watney's prolonged ordeal. Matt Damon has to perform much the movie alone, expertly conveying his character's intellectual reasoning without coming off as overly dry or talking down to the audience. One of the smartest sci-fi blockbusters of the 2010s, "The Martian" treats its premise well while celebrating intelligence to save the day.

One of the most prolific hard sci-fi authors was Arthur C. Clarke, who teamed up with filmmaker Stanley Kubrick for "2001: A Space Odyssey." The 1968 movie traces humanity's evolution through a strange extraterrestrial monolith that first appeared on Earth during prehistoric times. When a monolith found on the Moon transits a signal to Jupiter, an expedition is mounted to investigate further. This voyage is nearly derailed by the malevolent artificial intelligence HAL 9000 (Douglas Rain) running the team's spaceship.

Given Kubrick's exhaustive attention to detail and Clarke's scientific acumen, "2001: A Space Odyssey" is as hard as the genre gets on film. For as many confusing moments that the movie has, it keeps the audience riveted with its solid grounding. What makes the movie work is its juxtaposition of realistic sci-fi and existential pondering, balancing hard science with cosmic introspection. The best Stanley Kubrick movie, "2001: A Space Odyssey" brings out the best in its filmmaker and co-writer to bring this spacefaring tale to life.

A new season of the HBO series The Gilded Age is currently heating up on the 2026 TV schedule with all the social climbing, relationship drama, and elaborate costumes that it’s become known for. I’ve been watching it since the beginning, when audiences were first introduced to Enid Turner, an ambitious woman serving as Bertha Russell’s lady’s maid.

Back then, the woman only known as Turner learned quickly that if you’re going to cross Bertha (Carrie Coon), you’d better have enough standing to back it up. Turner did not and became a villain to the Russell family. If you had told me then that same character would evolve into my favorite in Season 4 of the HBO series, I never would have believed you. That would also just mean that I didn’t have the same faith in Enid as she had in herself.

Played with so many layers by Kelley Curran, Enid instantly became a character that I loved to hate but always felt like there was more under the surface. Sure, she attempted to seduce Bertha Husband, George Russell (Morgan Spector), which was a no-no for his wife, ultimately leading to her downfall within the household. The fact that she knew she was better than that kept her clawing her way up the social ladder as she returned, season after season, eventually becoming the character I now can’t help but root for.

In Season 2 of The Gilded Age, Enid seemed to have finally caught a break, marrying Joshua Winterton for financial security and a more prominent place in society. Being significantly older and in ill health led to his death, but it also left his fortune in Enid’s hands, and she was very savvy when it came to using it to the fullest extent of the social-climbing ladder.

Yet somehow, that wasn’t the end of Enid’s story. It has reached even higher with the delicious fun in Season 4. Now married to the not-very-secretly gay Oscar Van Rhijn (Blake Ritson), the duo has formed a partnership with a shared goal of social domination. Together, they plot and plan with devilish schemes that I’ve found myself rooting for with delight.

As a character, Enid is a magnificent sleight-of-hand magician, creating illusions and deceptions as she rises in social ranks. She is the definition of fake it until you make it, going toe-to-toe with her one-time rival at an upcoming lavish dinner that you must stay tuned for in Episode 5, airing on November 29.

While Marian and Larry can’t seem to get on the same page in Season 4, Enid and Oscar might not have romance between them, but being similar in age and mentality means they can understand and support each other in ways neither has had before. It allows her moments to shine with the confidence needed to not only take on Bertha but finally gain the upper hand.

The Gilded Age cast is truly stacked with talent, but what Kelley Curran has been able to do over four seasons, turning a hated villain into a powerful figure that viewers can root for, has been fascinating, fun, and entirely surprising to watch. It’s early in the season for this HBO show that got the world talking, and there’s quite a bit of Enid’s journey still to go, but you can watch all the drama on Sunday nights or with an HBO Max subscription.

Amazon has dropped the price of the two-pack Netgear Orbi 770 Series Wi-Fi 7 Mesh System to $449.99 from $549.99, saving you $100 on a setup that includes a router and a satellite node, with a combined coverage area of up to 5,500 square feet. If you don't need quite as much coverage, smaller configurations, including a single satellite node, is also discounted as part of Amazon's early Black Friday sale. It now costs $239.99, down from $349.99, and covers up to 2,750 square feet.

The system uses tri-band Wi-Fi 7 technology to spread your connection across three bands, with combined speeds of up to 11,000Mbps. It also supports wider 320MHz channels, though you'll need compatible Wi-Fi 7 devices to take advantage of those faster connections. If you prefer wired connections for devices that need a more stable link, the main router has three 2.5GbE LAN ports and a 2.5GbE WAN port, while the satellite offers two 2.5GbE LAN ports. This gives you plenty of room to connect a gaming console, desktop PC, or smart TV, and you can also use wired backhaul if your home has Ethernet cabling.

Once everything is connected, you can handle setup and day-to-day management through Netgear's Orbi app, while a web dashboard offers additional settings (for anyone who wants more control over their network), including VPN access and port forwarding, notes this PCMag review. There's no USB connectivity or 10GbE support, and some of its more advanced security and parental control features require a separate subscription after a free 30-day trial. Its Smart Parental Controls, for instance, cost $7.99 per month or $69.99 annually.

#3447. James Gunn Addresses Rumors Of Skydance Changes To Superman Sequel Man Of Tomorrow

News that James Gunn and Peter Safran would be "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads shocked the industry. At this stage, there's been no official word on what might become of Gunn's DC Universe, but there has been all sorts of conjecture and rumors making the rounds. One of these rumors suggests that the upcoming "Superman" sequel, "Man of Tomorrow," will be significantly reworked ahead of its 2027 release. Now, Gunn has taken to social media to quash the rumor — though at this point it's hard to know who to believe.

Following the Warner Bros./Paramount merger, DC Studios now belongs to Skydance, and it seems the new ownership has big changes in store. Reports have claimed that Skydance CEO David Ellison will dismantle Gunn's DC Universe following his departure. Meanwhile, Nexus Point News published an article in which it cited sources claiming "Man of Tomorrow" is being trimmed down ahead of its July 2027 release. According to the outlet, planned cameos are being cut and reshoots being planned. If Ellison is, indeed, planning to raze Gunn's cinematic universe, that would make sense. According to Gunn himself, however, it's all nonsense. The director wrote a post on Threads stating:

"There are a lot of untrue rumors going around, but one of them is that Skydance has seen 'Man of Tomorrow' and that all sorts of sweeping changes are being made. No one from Skydance has even seen the movie — the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. So any stories around this narrative are false."

On one hand, it's reassuring to hear that James Gunn will be able to finish his movie without Skydance making changes. On the other, he didn't actually state unequivocally that the new owners wouldn't be altering "Man of Tomorrow," only that nobody from Skydance has seen the movie yet. But given what we're hearing about how David Ellison plans to reboot the DC Universe, and the fact he's appointed a new DC Studios head in Jeremy Latcham, it would make sense for "Man of Tomorrow" to be reworked.

Gunn previously confirmed that Xolo Maridueña's Blue Beetle would return in "Man of Tomorrow." Nexus Point News' report claims that this is one of the cameos on the chopping block following Skydance's Warner takeover. If true, it would frankly make a lot of sense. Ellison clearly has plans for DC moving forward, and he won't want audiences confused by cameos that suggest the return of erstwhile heroes to a universe he plans to dismantle.

Page Six has reported that Gunn is only staying to finish "Man of Tomorrow" because Directors Guild of America rules mean he "could not be removed" from the project. If accurate, this suggests Ellison would have given Gunn the boot from his own movie if he could — adding more credence to the idea that Skydance wants to make changes to "Man of Tomorrow" and the DC Universe as a whole.  According to the director himself, this is all untrue. But everything we've seen and heard suggests otherwise.

A Puck report has claimed that James Gunn and Peter Safran's DC Studios exit was driven in part by cost-cutting. Given all the financial promises David Ellison had to make in order to close the Warner/Paramount merger, and the fact Gunn and Safran were making a tidy little profit for themselves via a deal that gave them significant autonomy as DC Studios co-heads, that makes sense. As such, if Skydance is committed to putting out "Man of Tomorrow," it will want to do all it can make sure it's profitable while also trying not to misguide audiences with cameos and setups for a DC Universe future that simply isn't going to arrive.

It's unclear whether the same rules that supposedly prevented Skydance from removing Gunn from "Man of Tomorrow" will also prevent them from meddling too much in the final product. But it seems almost certain that Ellison will want to have some say in the movie. With Jeremy Latcham now set to oversee DC Studios, clearly the Skydance CEO has a different vision in mind for the brand moving forward. The fact that nobody from Skydance has seen "Man of Tomorrow," therefore, doesn't necessarily mean they don't have major changes planned.

Bearing in mind Gunn and Safran were previously told they would be staying on at Skydance before Ellison suddenly dropped the axe, it's hard to say who knows what over at DC Studios. For now, Gunn clearly believes he'll be able to put out the "Superman" sequel he wants to make, but who's to say what might happen over the coming months. "Man of Tomorrow" is set for a July 9, 2027 release, and a lot can happen between now and then.

#3446. Forget Ganon, Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s Most Overlooked Boss Finally Gets Its Due

The age of Ganon is over. It's Twinrova's turn to rule

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is iconic for plenty of reasons, but a big part of that is thanks to its villain. Ganondorf is one of gaming’s great bad guys, a reputation that has only been enhanced by appearances in later games like Wind Waker and Tears of the Kingdom. While Ocarina of Time’s Switch 2 remake does the Demon King justice, it’s also a reminder that the Zelda series has another excellent, and far more underappreciated, foe: Twinrova.

First introduced in Ocarina of Time, Twinrova makes for one of the best bosses in Zelda history. In the Spirit Temple, Link encounters two evil sorceresses who serve Ganondorf, Kotake and Koume. They’re classic witches: a pair of bickering old ladies flying around on brooms. The character concept is fun enough on its own, but the fight itself is memorable, too. Link has to use his Mirror Shield to absorb their elemental attacks (fire and ice) and reflect them back at the witches. It all culminates with the duo coming together Transformers-style to become Twinrova, an even more powerful witch.

The sisters’ real star-turn moment happens after Link vanquishes their Twinrova form and they separate once more. Halos appear above both witches’ heads as they begin floating up towards a light. That sets them off into a panic as they realize they are dying, prompting an unexpectedly great sketch comedy routine.

Koume: We’re twins! Don’t try and lie about your age!

Koume: Who are you calling senile?! Is that how you treat your older sister?

Kotake: We are twins! How can you be older?

The remake not only preserves that screwball dynamic, but plays it up tenfold. The witches are fully voice acted, and they sound exactly as you probably always imagined, speaking in cartoon squawks. New animation lets Nintendo go all in on their final argument, as the two taunt and shove each other as they rise into the light. It’s a delightful moment of levity right before Link’s adventure gets serious en route to Ganondorf’s castle.

All of that has left me begging for Nintendo to lean on some Zelda villains other than Ganon in future games. Twinrova got a moment to shine as the big bad of the Oracle games, but they’ve rarely been seen in the 25 years since. There are a lot of villains like that who haven’t been revisited in decades while Nintendo keeps returning to Ganon: Agahnim, Vaati, Demise, Majora, and more. All of them are underexplored in Zelda’s mythos compared to Ganon.

There’s a case to be made, of course, that villains like Twinrova are so special because they’re not dragged out over and over again. They appear in games where they feel relevant to the story and design, so why force them into games just for the sake of fan service? Maybe Nintendo is better off creating new villains, like Echoes of Wisdom’s Null or A Link Between Worlds’ Yuga.

I can get behind that, though there is a good opportunity to revisit Twinrova if Nintendo decides to do so. You can spot the younger version of Koume and Kotake in Tears of the Kingdom, and they play a role in Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment. A new game set in that era, with some incarnation of Link facing off against them, could expand the Zelda mythos in a way that feels natural. After all, the witches are 400 years old (give or take) by the time we meet them in Ocarina of Time. I’m down to see what hijinks the siblings were getting up to at the young age of 104.

Nintendo’s excellent Switch 2 remake recaptures the soul of a masterpiece

#3445. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

In an age of prequels, sequels and reboots, I kind of expect most successful films to get at least one of those things. Weirdly, Tangled hasn’t. Yes, it is getting a live-action adaptation, and there was the animated series Rapunzel’s Tangled Adventure. However, it has not gotten an animated sequel to go along with the 2010 hit. Now, someone asked a Disney exec if there are any plans to ever make a Tangled 2.

Not long after the live-action Tangled wrapped production, and in the lead-up to the release of Disney’s newest animated project on the 2026 movie schedule, Hexed, Disney Animation’s chief creative officer, Jared Bush, was asked if there have been any discussions about Tangled 2. Here’s how he responded to Collider’s question:

We discuss all kinds of things all the time. I think people would be kind of surprised by the number of discussions we have around, ‘Do we want to return to a world with characters that we really care about?’ It's all the time for many, many different things. I think it always comes down to: Is there a filmmaker who is passionate and has a story that's undeniable that we must tell? That usually is how we approach any new story.

While Bush didn’t confirm or deny whether there have been talks about a Tangled sequel, it does seem like, to get one made, it would need to have a director leading the charge who cares deeply about it and a story that has to be seen on the big screen. Makes sense to me. I wouldn’t want to see a sequel to one of the best princess movies ever if it didn’t have those two things either.

Adding to that, the exec explained that Tangled is what drew him to the world of Disney. He also recalled how it revived the musical for them too, saying:

The world of Tangled is one of the things that drew me to Disney Animation. I think when that movie came out, there was this resurgence of the Disney musical. That's no easy feat. You may remember that when that movie came out, we weren't sure whether Disney musicals were something that people wanted to watch, and that said, ‘Yes, it's something that people want to watch — a new version of what that could be.’ So, it has a very special place in my heart. And Byron, my good friend, was one of the directors.

Overall, it sounds like the bar is very high for a Tangled sequel (as it should be), and maybe that’s why we’ve never seen one. However, considering we’ve gotten two Frozens and now they’ve gotten a third one off the ground, I will never totally give up on Tangled 2.

Plus, while we wait to see if that ever happens, we will not be devoid of Tangled content. In fact, we’ll get to see Teagan Croft and Milo Manheim take over as Rapunzel and Flynn Rider, respectively, in the live-action version in 2028. Seriously, the casting alone has me so stoked to see this take on the animated classic, and I’m sure it’ll be well worth the wait.

Now, as we continue to anticipate the live-action Tangled and dream about an animated Tangled 2, you can stream the original Tangled with a Disney+ subscription.

#3443. Keanu Reeves And Denzel Washington's Forgotten '90s Shakespeare Movie Is Worth Revisiting

Kenneth Branagh's 1993 film adaptation of William Shakespeare's "Much Ado About Nothing" is, without hyperbole, one of the best films of its decade. And what a cast! Denzel Washington plays Don Pedro, a soldier returning home from the war, bringing with him the handsome young Claudio, played by Robert Sean Leonard, and Don Pedro's grumpy, villainous half-brother Don John, played by Keanu Reeves.

Additionally, Branagh plays the sharp-witted Benedick, and stands romantically opposite Emma Thompson, playing the even sharper-witted Beatrice. The actors were married at the time, and their scenes together play like gangbusters. Claudio falls in love with the pretty young Hero, played by Kate Beckinsale. Michael Keaton turns in one of his funniest performances as Dogberry, a slovenly cop. Also keep an eye out for Imelda Staunton, Richard Briers, and the amazing Brian Blessed.

Branagh understood that Shakespeare's text was so aggressively light and frothy that he needed to make a film that matched its tone and spirit. As such, "Much Ado" is bright, brisk, pastoral, and gorgeous. Despite a plot involving staged infidelity, faked deaths, and bitter reactions, the movie is overall an injection of liquid sunshine. The bulk of the film is laughter, romantic shenanigans, playfully flirtatious barbs, and relaxing summer night parties in the Sicilian countryside. And, naturally, as a comedy, everything works out in the end. I want to live in this movie.

There have been other recent, passable film renditions of "Much Ado" in recent years, including Joss Whedon's 2013 version, which bore the filmmaker's unique voice, and the 2023 romantic blockbuster "Anyone But You" with Sydney Sweeney and Glen Powell, but neither can match the glories of Branagh's version. It remains the high-water mark for filmed versions of this play.

"Much Ado About Nothing" takes place in Messina, and opens with a glorious homecoming from Don Pedro and his men. This is a joyous occasion, and everyone in Messina is happy to begin a period of merry-making. It also marks the reunion of bitter exes Beatrice and Benedick, who seemingly hate each other, but who verbally spar so well, it's quite clear they're romantically perfect for each other. Each of their friends schemes to force Beatrice and Benedick back into each other's arms, largely by being "overheard" in choice situations.

Upon homecoming, Claudio instantly falls for the pretty young Hero, but he hasn't the wherewithal to charm her. Luckily, at a masked ball, Don Pedro stands in for Claudio, successfully charming Hero in his stead. A marriage is immediately arranged because this is Shakespeare, and comedies have to end with marriages. Meanwhile, side characters are hooking up left and right. "Much Ado" is a marvelously horny movie, and every actor looks the best they have ever looked.

Of course Don John is lurking in the shadows to foul everything up. He sees all the happiness at play and wishes to squelch it for reasons of generic villainy. He arranges for Claudio to witness a couple undressing in a window, convincing Claudio that he is witnessing Hero cheating on him already. Claudio, being a bit of a golden retriever, believes him and becomes bitter, rejecting Hero at the least opportune moment. And while there are some hard feelings of anguish, Branagh has already communicated through his film's bright white coloration, brisk music (by Patrick Doyle), and warm photography (by Roger Lanser), that everything is going to be fine.

The only real issue one might take with Branagh's "Much Ado About Nothing" is — and I hate to say it — Keanu Reeves' performance. Reeves is a capable actor in the right kind of taciturn roles, and he is one of the best human beings we have on planet Earth, but he clearly struggles with Shakespeare's language. After "Much Ado" was released, a notable parody of Reeves' performance was featured on the TV series "The Critic," wherein Reeves was mockingly placed in a film version of "The Merchant of Venice," intoning, "Hath not a dude eyes?"

But Reeves' performance aside, "Much Ado" is pretty damn perfect. The film currently has a 90% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 48 reviews. Roger Ebert gave the film three stars out of four, writing:

"Sunshine and laughter, and merrymakers on a hillside sprinkled with flowers. In the opening scene of 'Much Ado About Nothing,' Kenneth Branagh insists on the tone the movie will take: These are healthy, joyful young people whose high spirits will survive anything, even the dark double-crosses of Shakespeare's plot."

For a while there, Kenneth Branagh was on a hot streak. His 1989 debut feature "Henry V," also based on Shakespeare, was a critical darling, and his 1991 past-lives noir "Dead Again" is way better than it has any right to be. The '90s were very good for Branagh overall, as he also made "Peter's Friends" (1992), "Mary Shelley's Frankenstein" in 1994 (which is better than you remember and accurate to Shelley's novel), "In the Bleak Midwinter" (1995), and one of the very best movie versions of "Hamlet" in 1996. "Much Ado" was just a bright, soft, white feather in his feather-festooned cap.
