[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release “Paper Tiger” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

An actor who started at 22, Miles Teller earned rave reviews out of the gate for his debut performance in “Rabbit Hole,” when he was signed swiftly by CAA, followed by “Whiplash” and “The Spectacular Now.” He has worked steadily ever since, with everything from auteur fare like “Whiplash” and studio franchises such as “Divergent” and “The Fantastic Four” to his name. Holding his own opposite Tom Cruise in the blockbuster “Top Gun: Maverick” pushed him into the limelight, but he was still playing Rooster, the son of radar intercept officer Nick “Goose” Bradshaw (Anthony Edwards). Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

His latest role in James Gray’s “Paper Tiger,” which earned raves at Cannes, sees Teller play a real grown-up, Irwin Pearl, a Queens engineer and family man opposite Scarlett Johansson as his wife Hester, and Adam Driver as Gary, his older brother, a former cop. No longer the onscreen son of a leading man, Teller is now firmly in father roles. Irwin is slowly building a solid business when his brother offers a quicker route to success. Alas, the naive Irwin goes for the idea and, during an unscheduled night reconnaissance, blunders with the Russian mafia, seeing things he should not see.

I sat down with Teller at the Carlton Hotel in Cannes after the movie wowed in its world premiere. He was seeing it for the first time. We do not count fake standing ovations at IndieWire, but I was there and can vouch that it played well. The dynamic between Driver and Teller is powerful, with Johansson holding her own in the middle. Even though the movie did not land a Cannes prize, it will play the fall festivals and enter awards contention.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Anne Thompson: You’ve played the Cannes game before.

Miles Teller: I’m one of those actors [where] it’s pretty hard to watch yourself. I always have a hard time. I was here with Nic [Winding] Refn for this limited series that we did [“Too Old to Die Young”]; that was my first time at Cannes. I’ve done Cannes with “Maverick.” It’s truly an overload of the senses.

You’ve never given this kind of performance before.

Hopefully, your taste evolves as you get older. It struck me that on my first film, “Rabbit Hole,” I was playing the wide-eyed teenager, and we filmed the majority of that movie in a house in Queens. And now I’m playing the part of the parent.

That was your breakout. You revealed some strong emotions related to your own car accident. I’m so sorry you lost your home in the Palisades Fire.

When I met James for this movie, our house had just burned down. And I had just lost my grandfather. We were renting a place in Santa Barbara, and then I got the call saying James wanted to meet me for this. That infused this story and performance with a lot of love as well, because of that feeling of home that Keleigh [Sperry] and I had lost. I’d lost it with my grandfather, but then also just the physical place where you can have people come gather, where you have memories attached. We did not have that, so that probably came through.

Do you believe that you have to grow up a bit before you can find your way in Hollywood?

If you want to have a long career, the audience, hopefully, that you attract in your early 20s, as they get older, and they start having kids or not having kids, but just getting more life experience under the belt, you want to reflect that in your choices as well. And James makes movies for adults, he deals with characters. I’ve loved every one of his films, and I’ve always felt like he gets incredible performances, so I was excited to play a man at this point.

Every actor is going to get to a place where you know it’s tough because you do something that has some success to it, and then people want you to keep doing that same thing, whether that’s from the studio side or you keep getting scripts that are that same kind of thing.

When I started out with “Rabbit Hole,” and then I wanted to audition for comedy, they’re like, “he’s not funny.” And then you do comedies, and you want to be going back to drama, and they’re like, “Willard from ‘Footloose,’ what are you talking about?”

I remember “Bleed for This.” [He gets up to close the shutters to block the noise for my audio, and pours me some water.] That was a point where I was 27, and I said, “OK, I want to step up and play, not the funny friend. Playing Vinny Patz, as a five-time world champion boxer, very much a man’s man, absolutely, that was something. But it always comes down to a director, oftentimes taking what I feel is a chance on me, casting me in a role that I haven’t necessarily shown those abilities before, but believing that I could do that.

You had to carry the TV series “The Offer,” in which you play Al Ruddy, who produced “The Godfather,” running interference between Francis Ford Coppola, Robert Evans at Paramount, and the mafia. That must have been tough.

I was intimidated by portraying Al, to be honest with you, not just his bravado and accomplishments, but it felt like I was playing somebody who had more life experience than I had at that point, and there was a certain maturity to that. I enjoyed that Al, being a man of action, if he takes a step back, he’s taking two steps forward. Typically, there’s five or six different producers doing all these things: that was all Al.

In “Paper Tiger,” there’s one scene between you and Adam Driver where you get into a fight. Your face was shaking with anger.

I know. I saw that. Yeah, there was a twitch going on there. At least in my own life, your family can get to you in a way that nobody else can. Those feelings are so deeply rooted and established from childhood, so I guess in that moment, and neither one is fully aware of the ramifications of the Russians, this deal going bad, and how it’s affecting that person in their life. In that particular scene you’re letting out. It’s not just about what they’re talking about right there. It’s an entire lifetime of misgivings — he’s going to let him have it. When that’s happened to me in my personal life, you feel so bad afterwards. It’s a horrible feeling when you’re not talking to a sibling or your parents, and often it’s hard to make amends.

How did James Gray base this film on his own father’s experience?

With his father, that was the biggest regret. He took it to his deathbed, the fact that he brought this [danger] into his home, and his family became collateral damage for his business ambition. [In the movie] the venture that he went into, to go into business with his brother, he makes a mistake that was very naive. I think it’s easy to forgive this mistake. When I read this script, I had a ton of empathy for this family in this situation, and then also what Hester is going through.

Did you have any models for your character in this movie? Your own father was an engineer.

No, he was a project controls manager, but worked nuclear. The men that I grew up around, my father and my grandfather, were strong men, but very sensitive, and were dependable, reliable. My grandfather was married to my grandmother for 60-something years. I never saw her open a door for herself. I never saw her carry her own bag. He was a Marine, but he also was well-versed in world history, and he was a sweet man who was never afraid to show that side of him, but he also would stand up for himself, or his wife, or his kids, whatever it is. He took a lot of pride in that.

I found it refreshing, even comforting, to watch a movie about a kind, loving family man who’s good at his job, who’s competent. He’s a good dad. You haven’t shown that side to such a degree.

I felt immensely for this father and husband. It was clear he loves his kids, and he’s trying to lead by example, and to show them that success in life is not based on the car you drive. He wants to show them that you can build something on your own merit, and if you work hard and treat people right, that you can earn it.

Those values are no longer as respected as they once were. So, if you were to look back at your career, you did some studio work, like the “Divergent” series. Have you made a course correction? That comes with maturity, too, when an actor recognizes what they want to do rather than doing what people tell them to.

Early on, I didn’t want to feel like I was repeating what I had just done. I didn’t want people to be able to expect what I was going to do next. I always want to defend young actors in their careers, because people say, “Oh, why did you make that choice? Why did they make that choice?” You’re just hoping to get a role, and it’s less than 10 percent of people in SAG who pay their bills off acting alone. We all want to work on the best material with the best directors and the best actors. There’s an ebb and flow. I used to be more critical of work other people were doing, because you get thrown into this rat race when you’re first starting out.

Who were you competing with? Who was in your class?

It was me, and Michael B. [Jordan] and [Robert] Pattinson and Shia [LaBeouf] and [Zac] Efron was big, “The Hunger Games” stuff was blowing up. As I’ve gotten older, I appreciate and have respect for longevity, if you can hang around. I always wanted to contribute. When I was going to the Lee Strasberg Institute at NYU, and looked on the wall, there’s all these incredible actors that went through there. I hold acting and actors in such high regard, whether it’s theater or film or TV.

You seem to be delivering performances at such a level that you keep getting more work. The work itself is selling you. You had to counteract some bad press. Did that hurt you in terms of getting roles?

That was so mishandled. The reason why I have not done profiles is because I said, “Wow, if I’m not doing this interview on camera, this person can misquote things or put things out of order or say things that didn’t happen.” It felt like such a violation of what actually transpired. I told my team, “Guys, I don’t think I’m doing this again, because I’m reading this and this doesn’t sound like me to me. This is not life, so why would I ever want to be a part of something where they can just put that in?” So it’s unfortunate that being a good person, that doesn’t sell. People want to click on the negativity. If you go to bed and put your head on your pillow and how you treat people truly, that’s what matters. That [2015] interview was like 12 years ago.

Some people still remember. Well, casting directors know who you are and what you can do.

The actors, the directors, the crew, the producers, you can’t hide who you are when you’re on set.

Legal questions surround the Michael Jackson estate and his lawyer, John Branca, who you play in “Michael,” which has grossed $707 million worldwide. What’s going on with the sequel?

They had to rework the third act of the last movie. As far as the sequel goes, I know they’re working on it. I haven’t had any direct discussions, other than the team is excited to complete that story.

#3406. 15 Years Later, Jamie Lannister’s Best Game of Thrones Quote Is an All-Time Fantasy Hit

Jamie remains a fan-favorite for a reason

Many factors have helped make George R.R. Martin’s A Song of Ice and Fire one of the most beloved fantasy series of all time, and one big reason is HBO’s adaptation of the dark fantasy epic by showrunners David Benioff and D. B. Weiss. The eight-season adaptation brought Martin’s vast, stunning world and complex central characters to life. Jaime Lannister, played by Nikolaj Coster-Waldau, was one such character. And like many others in Game of Thrones, he had poetic one-liners that captured his nature and helped define his place in the story over the years.

Unlike Ned Stark, whose blunt and severe demeanor left little room for elaborate remarks, Jaime Lannister seemed to have an arsenal of memorable quotes and cutting one-liners. His words reflected both his standing as Tywin Lannister’s beloved son and as Lord Commander of the Kingsguard, as well as the complicated reputation he carried throughout Westeros. To many, Jaime was a man without honor, and his sharp remarks often seemed to echo the way others judged him.

With so many banger quotes from Jaime, it’s tough to pick the best one. Still, we think we’ve narrowed it down to a line that captures a key part of Jaime’s character and a central fantasy theme.

Of all the meaningful lines Jaime delivers over Game of Thrones’ eight seasons, one perfectly highlights a key theme that often serves as a source of strength in stories, regardless of genre: love. Martin, however, twists that theme in a way that helps ensure Jaime goes down as one of fantasy’s most memorable characters.

In the show's first episode, “Winter is Coming,” Jaime delivers his best line to his sister, Cersei, shortly after Bran Stark, the youngest son of Ned Stark of House Stark, catches them locked in an incestuous romantic embrace in one of Winterfell's towers.

Turning to Cersei, Jaime gives a self-assured smirk and says:

Moments later, Jaime pushes Bran out the open window — triggering a chain of events that leads to eight seasons of warfare, seedy politicking, and epic fantasy unlike anything ever seen before.

Love is a powerful emotion that drives stories across every genre and format. It is love that causes Jack to sacrifice himself for Rose in Titanic, and it is love that protects Harry from dying from Voldemort’s killing curse in Harry Potter.

Game of Thrones may be a dark fantasy tale in which nobody is truly safe, but that does not mean its characters are one-dimensional. Both D&D and Martin have made it clear that even the most loathsome among them can feel love and form deep attachments.

Those feelings do not necessarily make them kinder or less dangerous. On the contrary, in some cases they will commit monstrous acts for the people they love. That is clearest with Jaime, who is capable of killing a boy if it means his secret relationship with Cersei isn’t exposed to the rest of Westeros.

Jaime committing heinous acts for the love of his sister proves just how obsessive and toxic that love can be. It’s only when Jaime realizes his sister cares more about power than about being with him that he eventually wises up.

Unfortunately, Jaime’s toxic bond with Cersei has been a foundational part of him since childhood. Even when Jaime eventually leaves Cersei’s influence and forms a romantic relationship with Brienne of Tarth, sleeping with her after the Battle of Winterfell, it’s not enough. When Jaime hears of Cersei’s precarious situation in King’s Landing in the final season, he abandons Brienne and the Starks to rush back to the capital to try to save Cersei from her own folly.

Ultimately, this final act of love for his sister leads to Jaime’s downfall. Even as the Red Keep begins to crumble, Jaime refuses to leave Cersei’s side. They came into the world together, and so it only makes sense that they leave it together too.

As Aemond Targaryen explained to Jon Snow in A Game of Thrones: “We are only human, and the gods have fashioned us for love. That is our great glory, and our great tragedy.”

#3405. Jensen Huang’s Biopic Feels Inevitable — The Right One Might Be Impossible

Hollywood loves a visionary, especially one whose biggest gamble eventually made him a billionaire. But the trouble with making a biopic about a tech mogul actively shaping the future? That kind of story often refuses to sit still long enough to be told before ending in calamity.

When it comes to Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, any filmmaker hoping to get ahead of the microchip company’s uncertain next chapter may already be too late. Or is it still… too early?

On Thursday, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as CEO and board member, effective immediately. And no reason was given for the departure: a rather extraordinary development for someone who helped build the company into one of the most powerful and lucrative forces in artificial intelligence. For Hollywood, it’s the kind of twist that practically demands a screenplay. Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

Huang’s rise from teenage Denny’s employee to the face of the AI boom always had the makings of a prestige drama. Now there’s a corporate disaster — involving an alleged Chinese espionage operation and reports of multiple extramarital affairs — at the end of it. Hot dog! Still, it’s anyone’s guess whether that fiery conclusion can seem genuinely relevant by the time film and TV creatives get around to adapting it.

The entertainment industry has spent much of 2026 demonstrating how difficult it is to dramatize Silicon Valley while the real people involved keep making headlines. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” for example, opened to just $5.5 million in North America. That’s a disappointing debut for the follow-up to David Fincher’s “The Social Network,” which won three Oscars including best adapted screenplay.

Revisiting Facebook through the perspectives of whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), Sorkin attempted to turn Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) and his social media platform’s disastrous effects on politics and public discourse into a satisfying sequel.

Of course, audiences had already spent years living with the very real consequences of Zuckerberg’s company’s actions. And in his “D+” review for IndieWire, Ryan Lattanzio described Sorkin’s approach as “less old-fashioned than completely out of date,” criticizing a falsely triumphant finale that failed to reconcile how little had actually changed in the world after the investigation’s revelations came to light.

While Sorkin was late to the party, Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” has had the good fortune of arriving right as things have been starting to get worse. Dramatizing OpenAI’s chaotic 2023 firing and rehiring of Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield), the dark comedy finds absurdity in the gap between Big Tech’s grandiose promises and the frequently clownish folks making them.

In his “B-” review for IndieWire, David Ehrlich praised the coming film for recognizing how “deeply fucking stupid the road to superintelligence has turned out to be.” He also questioned its tendency to simplify an ongoing story into something more resolved than it is. (Suffice to say, any film that tries to predict the cultural conversation also risks declaring history finished too soon.)

“Artificial” has benefited from some remarkable timing, too. Amazon MGM dropped the project after entering into a partnership with OpenAI — with sources telling the Los Angeles Times that the script’s critical perspective on artificial intelligence specifically contributed to the decision. Neon eventually acquired it, and a well-received New York Film Festival premiere helped build some serious awards-season momentum for routine Oscar contender Guadagnino.

Then came the U.S. midterms, during which voters across the country backed restrictions on data-center development. That makes the questions about who controls AI and who actually pays for its consequences feel spectacularly urgent, effectively turning a simple boardroom fight into a existential consideration of society with significantly heavier stakes.

Of course, tech biopics don’t necessarily have to predict the future to be powerful.

Consider Hulu’s “The Dropout,” which won Amanda Seyfried an Emmy for playing Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Four years later, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s boundary-breaking documentary “You Can See Everything” once again made Holmes a viral sensation — even bringing Seyfried into contact with the woman she portrayed.

As IndieWire TV critic Ben Travers recently argued, “The Dropout” remains effective precisely because it didn’t pretend to know everything about Holmes in 2022. Fielder and Oppenheim’s contribution often gets so close to its subject that Holmes’ motives become difficult to pin down, while the series maintains enough separation to keep her actions and victims in focus.

“Sometimes a healthy distance provides greater clarity,” Travers wrote.

That’s a useful lesson for anyone hoping to next adapt the life of a Silicon Valley billionaire before history has finished passing judgment on them. And in Huang’s case, there’s already plenty of material to work with — before pretending to know how his former employer’s whole saga ends.

Having cofounded Nvidia in 1993, Huang nearly lost the company after betting on a method of rendering video-game graphics that Microsoft effectively rendered obsolete. With Nvidia running out of money, he then scrapped its original technology and made a last-ditch gamble on a new chip that ultimately helped save the business.

Huang eventually helped develop the graphics-processing infrastructure that would make his company’s hardware essential to the AI boom. Fast-forward to a public apology to his wife and throw in a leather jacket? Hollywood could probably have a trailer ready by Christmas.

But that would also be the easiest, and potentially least interesting, version of Huang’s story, right? Nvidia’s success was built on the backs of countless engineers, researchers, and developers aside from Huang. The fallout within the AI giant will impact everyone.

A truly great movie about Huang and Nvidia would need to understand the company’s founding and survival, follow the enormous risks Huang took with that future, and then seriously interrogate what happens when a single corporation becomes indispensable to the technology rapidly reshaping nearly all of modern life. Those are three(!) very different artistic ambitions. Considering the entertainment industry’s own increasingly lucrative partnerships with AI companies, and Amazon’s offloading of “Artificial,” there’s reason to wonder just how much scrutiny Hollywood would be willing to apply to the innovators they are in business with.

Which brings us back to the question of when to make a Jensen Huang biopic.

The tech industry is moving faster than filmmakers can reasonably hope to keep up with, but the bigger problem may be that news around the Silicon Valley story most worth telling is changing just as quickly. A film about the man who helped build the future we’re facing might have been an easy sell a few years ago. These days, the more pressing issue is what kind of world Huang actually put in motion — and whether Hollywood can afford to doubt it in public.

#3404. Patrick Stewart Had A Small But Important Role In One Of The Best Animated Movies Of The '90s

It feels impossible to do justice to the late Sir Patrick Stewart with mere words, but we can attempt it. One part of his incredible legacy is voice acting; how could he not try his hand there when he had such a magnificent voice? Stewart's defining voice role is probably the eccentric CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock on "American Dad." Casting him against type there is the whole joke. Patrick Stewart, famous for playing dignified, fatherly authority figures like Captain Jean-Luc Picard and Professor Charles Xavier, is the one saying all of Bullock's ridiculous, profane, and unhinged lines, which become even funnier read in his baritone voice.

The folks behind the biblical epic "The Prince of Egypt" also knew the weight Stewart's voice carried. At Steven Spielberg's suggestion, DreamWorks Animation adapted the first stretch of the Book of Exodus, or how the prophet Moses (Val Kilmer) — raised as an Egyptian prince — discovered his true heritage and led his people out of bondage. Patrick Stewart plays Pharaoh Seti, adoptive father of Moses and the man who ordered the massacre of Hebrew babies that made Moses' mother send him away. Stewart/Seti has only a few scant scenes in the movie's first act, but he casts a shadow as wide as any pyramid over the rest of the film.

As with later DreamWorks pictures, "The Prince of Egypt" employs celebrity voice casting: Kilmer as Moses, Ralph Fiennes as Moses' brother/Seti's son Pharaoh Rameses, etc. But here, it mostly works — mostly. Jeff Goldblum as Moses' brother Aaron is a distracting bit of casting where you hear the actor first, not the character. "Prince of Egypt" doesn't disguise Stewart's voice either (you probably couldn't with a voice of such power), but it complements his character to a chilling effect.

In "The Prince of Egypt," Seti first appears admonishing his two sons for being reckless in a chariot race. He's especially harsh on his heir, Rameses, explaining that "one weak link can break the chain of a mighty dynasty." When Moses asks his father to go easier on Rameses, Seti offers understanding (and pure dramatic irony): "Moses, you will never have to carry a burden like the crown I will pass to Rameses."

Pretty typical Patrick Stewart, right? Seti is stern but reasonable, some of the same qualities that made Captain Picard such a respected leader. His respect-commanding voice is even more effective as a disappointed father, too; would you want to hear "I'm disappointed in you" from that voice?

But then Moses learns the truth about where he came from, and how. Seeing his son in despair, Seti is gentle but also doesn't deny he had a generation of Hebrew babies murdered as population control. The animation and Stewart's performance work in perfect sync. In Seti's whispered tone, he sounds genuinely pained. Even if his claim "sometimes, for the greater good, sacrifices must be made," rings hollow here, Seti's thousand yard stare tells us that maybe he does feel the weight of what he did and realizes he's damned for it.

But then the kicker comes: He tries to "comfort" Moses that the babies cast into the Nile "were only slaves." The dissonance of Seti loving his own family and also being a genocidal enslaver is potent, but sadly believable. Fittingly, this is also the last time we see him in the film, because the bond he shared with Moses has been severed.

"The Prince of Egypt" is one of the most gorgeously animated films ever made, and it's not only the animation that's beautifully crafted. The storytelling is sharp and mature. It sits at the very fine line of being simple enough for kids and complex enough for adults; Moses and Rameses being turned from beloved brothers to enemies by forces much bigger than themselves is painful to watch.

Right off, "The Prince of Egypt" is an unconventional title for the Exodus story; after all, the whole story is about Moses rejecting that life for his people by birth. (Compare it to the 1956 biblical epic titled "The Ten Commandments.") But the movie paints Moses' deliverance of his people as bittersweet, since it cost him the brother he loved.

Though not nearly as controversial as Nikos Kazantzakis's book (and later Martin Scorsese's film) "The Last Temptation of Christ," "The Prince of Egypt" similarly invents human drama from scripture. "Last Temptation" works from the tenet that Jesus was both fully divine but also fully human. So, then, wouldn't he be afflicted by man's foibles and doubts? The Book of Exodus holds that Moses was raised as an Egyptian in the Pharaoh's own family. Wouldn't Moses, then, feel pained about having to turn his back on the home where he was raised, even if he recognized the necessity of God's plan for him?

Part of the tragedy is that this only flows one way. After Moses learns the truth, he can't look at the enslaved Hebrew workers without thinking their birthright is also his. Conversely, neither Seti nor Rameses clock that the son/brother they love would've been just another of those slaves. It's an excellent use of Patrick Stewart, twisting our relationship to his fatherly presence and providing an undercurrent of darkness to it.

#3403. ’12 12 12′ Review: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Ticking-Clock Heist Thriller Runs on Broken Time

Every episode of “12 12 12” opens with the same explanation of its title: Citing the fictitious law enforcement manual, “Principles of Crime, FBI Research Center, 4th Edition,” Anthony Mackie explains, “A high asset robbery, professionally conceived, is 12 months in planning, 12 hours in execution. A bank robber who’s not caught within 12 days is not caught at all.” Then the screen splits horizontally to reveal images from the 12 months of preparation, the 12 hours of execution, and the 12 days when thief extraordinaire Paul Galvin (Jamie Dornan) does his best to elude Mackie’s obsessed FBI agent Jack Strickland. And then, we’re off to the races. Related Stories ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

The heist genre, in theory, seems ripe for this kind of temporal manipulation. A game of wits between cops and criminals typically involves plenty of twists, many of which pull the rug out by flashing back to show where, when, and how it was placed so stealthily underfoot. Also working in “12 12 12’s” favor is the genre’s familiarity: There will be “getting the team together” montages, there will be unexpected hiccups in the days and hours during the robbery, there will be chest-thumping meetings between our confident cop and the equally confident con artist. Throw in the complex heist itself and the tense escape soon after, and there appear to be enough recognizable pieces that jumbling them up shouldn’t prove too confusing.

And “12 12 12” isn’t confusing. It is, however, convoluted. Taking a serpentine route through well-trodden territory does more to undermine our enjoyment of an otherwise well-mounted chase than it does to liven things up. Heists are inherently exciting. They’re exciting in conception (when master thieves can wow us with their slick plans), they’re exciting to see carried out (when the shit hits the fan and even the most astute architects have to think on their feet), and they’re exciting to get away with (when safety is within reach, but it could be snatched away at any moment). Anticipation, suspense, and anxiety work to form a natural arc, and disrupting that arc over and over, every hour for eight hours, in service of a few extra twists — and to extend what’s obviously a movie-length story across eight hours — simply isn’t worth it.

On that note, let me get this minor but essential point out of the way now, quickly and clearly: Jamie Dornan needs more weird roles, not more conventional ones. We saw what he can do in “Barb and Star Go to Vista Del Mar” (a modern comedy classic). Let the man cook — or sing or dance or all three at once! He can do it! Honestly, I believe he can do anything. (Remember the bee movie?! No, not that bee movie — the other one.)

Anyway, here his character’s only unique attribute is his brilliant… planning. He’s got a mind for details, and he uses it to map out every possible contingency before embarking on his elaborate heists. Caught in a bind with his dumbass brother (Jack Kesy, doing his best Travis Kelce impression), Bobby lays it out in aptly blunt terms: “Paul, you’re the fucking plan guy, so plan me a plan.”

But the only plans Paul wants to make these days are for his family: He’s happy working on fishing boats off the coast of France and coming home to his wife, Severine (Agathe Rousselle), in their little apartment above a bar. He’s bonded with his father-in-law, Serge (José Garcia), who’s the Marxist papa Paul never had, and he’s got a kid on the way.

Unfortunately, Bobby can’t stop being Bobby and winds up indebted to the wrong people; people who don’t just want their money back, but who want more money to make up for the inconvenience. And since Bobby already owes more money than either brother could ever pay back, Paul has to take on one last job to free his brother — and himself — from their lives of crime.

Too bad that puts him back on Jack’s radar or, I should say, squarely on Jack’s radar, since Jack is nursing a (secret) grudge against Paul from years earlier. Ever since, he’s been obsessed with catching the one criminal who’s eluded his grasp. He wants revenge, he wants “respect,” he wants to win — “12 12 12” throws out a number of motivations for Jack early on that clearly don’t paint the full picture. They’re placeholder reasons until the show deems it time to dig into what’s really driving him to move to Zurich, hole up in a shitty police station, and wait for Paul to try to steal something.

Mackie, who’s reunited with his “Falcon and the Winter Soldier” director Kari Skogland, gives great determined face, and Dornan is the softest, sweetest guy on the FBI’s most-wanted list. Thankfully, co-creators Dudi Appleton and Jim Keeble don’t ask their lead characters to betray their core identities amid all the twists and turns, shading Jack as more of an antagonist (all-consumed and, thus, single-minded to a fault) and Paul as more of the protagonist. (He doesn’t want to steal, but now that he must, he’s going to do it the right way.) That helps keep our rooting interests in line, which goes a long way toward a satisfying emotional payoff, even when the momentum ebbs and flows with every flash-forward, -back, and -sideways.

With slick locations and clever-enough problem-solving, “12 12 12” should satisfy die-hard heist fans (but not “Die Hard’s” heist fans). It just takes a circuitous route to scratching that itch, and that’s almost as aggravating as not scratching it at all.

“12 12 12” premieres Friday, November 13 on Apple TV with two episodes. New episodes will be released weekly through the finale (Episode 8) on December 25.

#3402. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3401. I Ain't Got No Body: The Various Non-Corporeal Aliens In Star Trek Explained

Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

One of the primary features of "Star Trek" is theoretical biology. Given the wide panoply of alien species on display throughout the franchise, audiences have been invited to ponder alternate evolutionary paths besides the one that happened to bring us into being on Earth. What kind of planetary conditions would be required to form, say, a hyper-intelligent crystalline being? How did a horta evolve? What will we evolve into in the future? Will our brains adapt to become psychic over time? According to the "Star Trek: Voyager" episode "Threshold" (one of the show's most outraging to fans), it was revealed that humans will eventually evolve into giant salamanders.

This leads to a few logical evolutionary extremes, like the fact that some species on "Star Trek" have evolved into beings of pure energy. "Star Trek" has many examples of non-corporeal aliens who can only be perceived as light, as a psychic presence, as a sound, or as a vision beamed directly into our inferior, corporeal brains. To cite a notable example: In the original series episode "Is There In Truth No Beauty?," audiences were introduced to the Medusans, a highly intelligent, telepathic, and empathic species whose light-constructed bodies are so wildly complex that any human looking at them would instantly go mad. Only a mentally disciplined species like the Vulcans could look at a Medusan, and even then required a special filtered visor (pictured above).

These kinds of aliens expand the audience's mind as to what can be considered life.

In looking at fictional non-corporeal species, "Star Trek" expands our horizons. We're invited to ponder new perspectives about basic concepts like evolution, time, the nature of consciousness, and, perhaps, our own relationship to the cosmos. Non-corporeal entities are one of the coolest ideas "Star Trek" has to offer, and their recurring nature is a constant reminder that life is more complex, and the cosmos more ineffable, than we could ever hope to imagine.

On "Star Trek," non-corporeal aliens tend to appear as lights or clouds or glowing mists of energy. One might recall the smoke-like alien that made Kirk nervous in the episode "Obsession," one of the more underrated episodes of the show. Others might immediately think of Zefram Cochrane's glowing, cloud-like "companion" in the episode "Metamorphosis." That entity had the ability to sort of intuitively communicate with Cochrane (Glenn Corbett), and could also heal diseases and sustain human life beyond its usual biological barriers. A common theme of non-corporeal entities on "Star Trek" is that they are godlike and powerful, able to tap into the powers of the universe in ways we don't understand.

The Medusans may be one of the most popular non-corporeal entities on "Star Trek," but fans of "Deep Space Nine" would surely want me to acknowledge the wormhole aliens, a.k.a. The Prophets. In that show's pilot episode, "Emissary," Benjamin Sisko (Avery Brooks) travels into a stable wormhole and encounters bodiless creatures who can only communicate with him by appearing as people from his memories.

The wormhole aliens from "Deep Space Nine" are so, well, alien, they don't understand concepts like linguistic communication or linear time. They don't see cause leading to effect, but rather a widespread series of events that happen all at once. Sisko has to do the impossible, and explain the human habit of seeing time as a straight line.

And, of course, there are many species of godlike beings on "Star Trek" who often take the form of humans, despite not having physical bodies. Q (John de Lancie) from "Star Trek: The Next Generation" is one of these beings, as is Trelane (William Campbell) from the original series. Those two beings tend to see corporeal humans as lesser species and amuse themselves by taunting and playing with them. Less whimsical is Kevin Uxbridge (John Anderson), a member of a powerful energy species called the Douwd. Kevin took the form of a human, married, and witnessed his wife killed, leading him to, in a moment of ill-temper, commit instant galaxy-wide genocide of a single species. He's the deadliest character in all of "Star Trek."

The list goes on. Q tormented the Calamarain, which exist as ionized gas. There are the Organians, the Lights of Zetar, and the godlike Metrons, the latter of whom oversaw the fight between Kirk (William Shatner) and the Gorn in the episode "Arena," and plenty of other examples. In most cases, non-corporeal entities are so far beyond human experience, it's difficult to communicate with them, much less come to some kind of diplomatic understanding.

But sometimes non-corporeal entities do become our friends. On "Star Trek: Prodigy," the character of Zero (Angus Imrie) is a Medusan who managed to construct a robot-like vehicle for themselves, allowing them to interact with us flesh-beings without exposing themselves. Sometimes the ineffability of the cosmos works in our favor.

#3400. Stardew Valley Meets Night in the Woods in One of 2026's Scariest New Games

I thought I knew what to expect from Village in the Shade after attending NIS America's pre-launch preview event in September. The villagers would be quirky but likeable, and things would probably get at least a little twisted, though nothing too terrible. Nippon Ichi Software's non-Disgaea games get pretty dark, as do the Labyrinth games and Yomawari. But they're dark on a small-scale, personal level, and rarely do they have something poignant to say. Village in the Shade tossed all my expectations out the window within the first few hours and, since then, has quickly rocketed up my list of the year's best games.

Village in the Shade starts with a child frolicking in the fields, running through dappled woods, skipping over rivers, and doing normal kid stuff. Then they fall down a hole and die, or so you'd think from the amount of blood on-screen, except they climb out and start walking again like nothing happened. Something did happen, though. The local carpenter and a hunter find the child, who happens to bear a striking resemblance to a kid who vanished years ago. Not that the idea brought anyone joy. They seem worried, actually, but Rin, the de facto mayor of Kagatsu Village, decides the child may be of use.

Rin initially seems like a Tom Nook caricature. She's fixated on profit and productivity, stuffs you in a ratty little hovel, charges you for it, and decides your value based on how much you do for the community. There's a bit of subtle commentary from her about min-maxing supposedly relaxing games to get the most out of them, and I thought this poke at established cozy staples would be the extent of Rin's personality. But NIS had something much more interesting in mind, which became evident the next in-game day when Rin threw a baby goat down the village well as an offering. One life out of the village in exchange for another life in. Balance must be maintained.

It likely comes as no surprise to hear this following a sentence that includes the words "threw a baby goat down the well," but Kagatsu Village is a weird place. A good quarter of the people who live there agree with that assessment. Even so, they don’t seem to have much of a choice but to stay and deal with it. Their families lived at the foot of this mountain for generations. Leaving would be tantamount to betrayal of everyone past and present, and who knows what might happen then?

Rin and Kagatsu Village under her rule are the epitome of toxic communalism. She's sincere in her dogged determination to put the village first — frighteningly so at times — but either overlooks or just plain doesn't understand the harm of ignoring the individual. Part of Kagatsu's code is that every favor must be met with appropriate compensation, which is great for people with mercenary dispositions. It’s less great if you just want to help a friend out with no strings attached. You're also not supposed to pry into anyone's affairs or share their secrets, no matter how upset they are or whether they're gathering poison as part of a murder plot. As long as the collective is intact and moving forward, every sacrifice is permissible. And mandatory.

The most common sacrifice is a monthly fee, like a tax, though to Rin's intense frustration, people tend to get around it. Some perform a service. Others give food or necessary items. Those with nothing to give, or who flat-out refuse to give anything, are taken to the local clinic where the doctor draws a rather alarming amount of blood. Blood figures quite prominently in Village in the Shade. There's the monthly offering, of course, along with a spate of serial killings 10 years in the past — around the time you disappeared from the village, in what's surely a totally normal coincidence. On some nights, one of the bridges leading to the center of town is covered in blood.

I'm a coward and haven't ventured beyond the bridge on those nights, so I don't know why the blood is there yet. Nighttime is dangerous in Kagatsu Village. Untold horrors slither down the mountain and haunt the streets and alleys, and dealing with them is much more nerve-wracking than I originally thought. The preview session showed the very first haunted incident, a linear segment where the ghost of an old man chases you through the village. It was pretty tame. The rest of the hauntings are not. Village in the Shade uses a drumming sound like a heartbeat and a tremor effect on the screen when danger approaches, and they increase in intensity the closer you get to the source of it. That, plus a general lack of defensive capabilities and places to hide, is enough to get the adrenaline going during evening wanderings. Stealth and bloody death were not on my bingo card when I started this game, and the intensity of these moments — plus just how at odds they are with the sedate daytime routine — make them standouts.

The "weird rural place with a terrible past" and its critiques on collectivism aren't entirely uncommon in Japanese media. Ryukishi07's Higurashi: When They Cry springs to mind as one of the stronger examples of it, and, more recently, there's The Summer Hikaru Died and even Nintendo's Emio — The Smiling Man. The concept is typically reserved for anime or visual novels, though, and I've yet to come across a good example of the storytelling style in more interactive media. Who'd have thought a farm-sim could make the perfect fit for it? Certainly not me.

But it does, and even the calm routine surprised me. Most farming games in the last decade have done very little to shake up the daily chores, and even Stardew Valley followed a pattern familiar from old Harvest Moon games. Village in the Shade holds little back at the start and throws a lot of crop variety, processing machines, and progress at you. I'd upgraded my tools once by the first summer, reached level 50 of the mine, and harvested enough spring crops to get them all to silver rank in quality.

It's not too easy, though, and NIS didn't skimp on the farming just to facilitate storytelling. In that first summer, I divided my fields (plural, as I bought a second one with my springtime earnings) into planned segments. There were flower fields for producing honey, flowers for selling, and a smaller plot for gift flowers. Crop-producing trees had a section all to themselves. The furrowed vegetables — Village in the Shade lets you alternate between tillage and furrows to encourage faster growth for some species — had a section all to themselves, just because uniformity looked nice.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

While I hadn't created rice paddies yet, that didn't stop me from spending thousands of yen on seedlings while the store had them in stock, and I created a special bed of edamame beans that I'd let ripen into autumn for a soybean harvest. Meanwhile, at the other end of the homestead plot sat my beehives, smelters, smithing station, mayonnaise maker, and pickling barrels. I had full access to cows, ducks, chicken, horses, and sheep despite being early in the game, too.

And all of this is for the good of the village. With more crops, more money, and more goods, you can fulfill more requests and improve Kagatsu, giving it a better chance at surviving into the future. Well, assuming there's enough people left to live there when the future arrives. Regardless of how things play out, I'm frankly astonished at just how well Village in the Shade tells its story and wraps it around familiar farm-sim routines. As we head into the twilight of 2026, this one definitely deserves a spot on the lists of the year's best games.

#3399. This Low-Profile Roborock Vacuum and Mop Is $500 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That said, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3398. In Shana Feste’s Films, Gender-Flipping Cinema’s ‘Tradition of Celebrating Damaged Men’ Is Its Own Reward

Shana Feste knows her filmography might be a bit tough to pin down. Some directors like to stick to a certain genre. Not Feste. Some only like to work with certain stars. Not Feste. Others enter a franchise and never look back. Not Feste.

But over the course of nearly two decades behind the camera, Feste has carved out a particular sweet spot, regardless of the genre or the cast or the wider world her stories fit inside: She likes complicated women. Not unlikable women, but messy women, contradictory women, women who get things done their own way. It’s a signature unto itself.

“My filmmaking, my history, people have not really known what to do with me. I’m making a comedy, I’m making a horror film, I’m making a genre thriller,” Feste told IndieWire during a recent interview. “But I do find that they’re all starting to build into each other, especially the trajectory from ‘Country Strong’ to ‘Run Sweetheart Run’ to ‘Heartland.’ I’ve always been drawn to women who don’t behave correctly. I’ve always been interested in women who don’t grieve correctly, who mother incorrectly, who love incorrectly. I just want women to have the freedom to behave in this contradictory, destructive, funny, selfish way and be given the same freedom that male characters are given.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

Another shared characteristic between Feste’s complicated women: They may be messy or unexpected, but they tend to get shit done. In her new film “Heartland,” getting shit done is at the center of the story, as the Nashville-set drama follows Jessica Chastain as Misty Jones, a former country-singing superstar who left the business after her designation as the, ahem, “cunt of country” became too much to bear. She’s thrust back into that world after her niece, rising star Charlie Heart (Carter Faith), goes missing. Misty, being Misty, takes it upon herself to get to the bottom of an increasingly dark and twisted mystery, no matter what it takes.

“I am a mom of three, 51, and I’m like, ‘Let’s write about some women who get shit done,’” she said. “I find a lot of those women exist. I’m living in the South now that I see those women every day and am inspired by them. We have this long-established cinematic tradition of celebrating damaged men. But when women behave similarly, they could be labeled as hysterical or dramatic or that word, unlikable. I want to prove that wrong.”

For the (complicated, messy, extremely capable) character of Misty, Feste said, she initially tapped into her longtime love of film noir. She always gravitated toward the Humphrey Bogart types, she said, but wondered what might happen if they gave those sorts of roles to women. That also fed into the dark underbelly of the Nashville scene that the film interrogates, a perfectly noir-ish idea.

“It could have been any city, but specifically this dark underbelly had to do with the music world,” Feste said. “Sadly, it was a common experience for a lot of artists that I spoke with. It was an experience that I’ve experienced in our industry, and it was all too relevant. When we were making the movie, a lot of conversation around Diddy was happening. He had just been arrested, and things were coming into light. We thought, oh wow, this is such a topical moment. And I’m like, it’s always topical, sadly. Whether we’re Epstein, Diddy, Weinstein, this is always going to be in the world, sadly.”

But Feste is also someone who loves this world and wants to celebrate what’s good and true about it. “Country Strong” was about making it — and maybe even making it again — even at great personal cost. “Heartland” just ratchets that sensibility up.

“I wanted to lean into the secrets and the dark corners and the underbelly, but I also will always celebrate the artistry and the storytelling of country music,” she said. “Misty says one line that really speaks so much to me about what the film is: ‘You don’t deserve country music.’ It takes a lot to deserve country music in my eyes. Country music is like the apex of storytelling. So to point out someone who doesn’t deserve country music, I mean, that’s a big insult for me.”

Feste started writing “Heartland” around four years ago, mostly because she was really missing the world of country music that framed her 2010 music drama “Country Strong.” “My father died about eight years ago, and I found myself listening to a lot of country music when he died,” she said. “In the years after he died, going back to the music that he loved, that he used to play for me in the car when we were driving on road trips, I realized that when you’re a writer, you don’t know quite why you write something until years later. And I realized, oh, I’m really missing my father.”

She was also eager to reteam with her “Country Strong” collaborators Jenno Topping and Randall Poster, two people who Feste said have believed in her the most over the course of her career. (Topping and Poster both produced “Heartland,” with Poster also serving as music supervisor, as he did on “Country Strong.”) “When I’m having my darkest days about, I don’t know, me and what I create and my career, knowing that they believe in me has always been such a huge lift,” Feste said. “So having them help me tell this story was just monumental. It was being with someone that you knew had your back the entire time.”

If “Heartland” sees Misty feeling ill at ease in the very spaces that used to celebrate her talent, Feste had the opposite experience. Six films into her directing career, she said “Heartland” let her approach her work in an entirely new way. And it felt good.

“What was really valuable with this experience is that I felt completely comfortable saying, ‘I don’t know,’ and I don’t know if I’ve ever felt that way,” she said. “Certainly not with my first few films, feeling like as a woman, I had to know every answer from every head of department immediately. It was only working with this group of filmmakers, Jenno and Randy and [production designer] Naomi [Shohan], some of my heads of production, that I knew that they saw my vulnerability not as a weakness, but as a strength. I was able to say, ‘I don’t know, what do you think?’ That’s where a very new form of collaboration happened that I haven’t experienced in my career, and with Jessica as well.”

Casting Chastain was an easy call for Feste. She wanted someone who could sing and who was admired in this space, but Chastain’s way of working and approach to on-set life gave Feste more to work with than she could have dreamed.

“I always want my films, especially when we’re shooting a movie that takes place in Nashville, to feel authentic, and I knew Jessica already had a huge buy-in from this audience. The South, they love her from ‘George & Tammy,’” Feste said. “And Jessica can sing, and that is another qualifier. Whenever I’m making any kind of movie with music, I want the actors to be able to sing their own material. But I think most of all, Jessica is one of the biggest champions of other women that I’ve ever met.”

It was freeing for Feste to say “I don’t know,” but Chastain also made it clear that she was there to support Feste’s vision and leadership.

“There were certain times on set where it would get a little loud or kind of disorderly, and people would be talking and having opinions, and no matter what, she’d be like, ‘Shana, sorry, I couldn’t hear you,’ and it was like this just gentle reminder, ‘This is who is leading the ship right now for me,’” the filmmaker recalled. “It was done in the classiest, most polite way.”

That approach turned the collaboration into more of a partnership. When Chastain had an idea, Feste was eager to listen. Even a decade ago, she said, that might not have been so easy for her.

“If I had been the director that I was 10 years ago, it would’ve scared me to death, because Jessica is not afraid to come into a scene and say, ‘OK, wait, that might not be serving us. Let’s throw that idea out of the window. What if we did this?,’” Feste said. “As a director, I’m planning, and every shot is in my head, and I’ve done the work, and I’ve done the homework, and I’m the A student. And to be able to relinquish control and admit when my idea wasn’t the best idea and she’s coming in with a stronger idea because she is Jessica Chastain? She has done the work. She has made this character so rich. This wasn’t a scary experience. It was actually going to elevate the scene and make it work even better.”

It was always the plan for Feste’s stars to also sing their songs to add to the film’s deeper authenticity. “When I’m watching movies that feature performing artists, and there’s so much hype, and they’re playing this celebrated musical performer, and then they come on, and we hear them sing and we’re like, have they been re-voiced? It’s just kind of mediocre? You just kind of lose your authenticity. You lose the ownership of the movie,” she said.

Casting Jennifer Nettles was something of a no-brainer for Feste, and so was actually directing the country superstar. “I didn’t know how to direct someone how to move on stage. That is something that’s not in my repertoire of directing. I can direct someone talking about their divorce in a bedroom, but how to command a stage and move your body? That is something that she learned over 20 years of experience being a superstar,” she said. “Most of the time I said, ‘Just speak to the audience like you are at the Opry, like you’ve done a thousand times. Make it your own.’ She did so much heavy lifting for me.”

So too did Carter Faith. In early discussions about the five characters in the film who are musical artists, Feste said she and Poster were constantly trying to figure out who they would sound like in the real world. Was Misty an Emmylou Harris? A Miranda Lambert? And who was young rising star Charlie Heart? Was she a Taylor Swift type? Poster had an easy answer: She sounds like this actual rising star, Carter Faith. And when it became clear that Faith was able to and interested in auditioning for the role? Serendipity.

“She was like a breath of fresh air,” Feste said. “I remember asking her, ‘Carter, what do you think you have in common with Charlie?’ And she said, ‘Well, we both have boy names.’ My heart exploded. It was the most non-Hollywood endearing response. Then I heard her story of how she was eating red beans and rice, crashing on couches, calling all of these places on Lower Broadway just to get an audition to be the performer at 10:00 AM on a Monday morning. She is someone who really moved to Nashville the day she graduated from high school to make it. She was Charlie. So much of her experience was exactly what the character was going through. So it was only the question of, are you brave enough to access all that trauma of how you got here? And she was absolutely, she said yes, and she trusted me, and it makes me emotional thinking about it because that’s an incredible trust to have.”

Faith also wrote the lyrics to the song that plays at the end of the film, which Feste sees as “dialogue that I could never write.” All the songs in the film and on its soundtrack, including the ones Feste simply imagined as titles first, like “Texas Land,” or that her stars like John Hawkes wrote or that Poster commissioned, add to the film’s incredible authentic feeling and sound. “Working with musical performances in film, it is so additive because it just takes the storytelling to another level. It’s beyond the dialogue. It’s beyond physical blocking. It tells story in this just purely emotional, raw, beautiful way,” she said.

Next up: In true Feste fashion, she’s working on or thinking about a variety of other projects next, including the next chapter of the “Dirty Diana” story, which she first cooked up during lockdown, a TV series about a Southern family, and her “dream project,” which is about Texas bank robbers. Mostly, she said, “I really want to continue working in this space. I want to continue telling stories about messy, complicated, vulnerable Southern women. I think that’s my bread and butter.”

#3397. This 75-inch Hisense Mini-LED TV Is Nearly Half Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 ahead of Amazon’s Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date. The rest of the U6 Pro lineup is discounted as well, so you can pick up the same TV in sizes from 55 inches to a massive 100 inches, for anyone with the room for something closer to a home-theater-sized screen. Whichever size you choose, you’ll get free delivery to the room of choice—a service that normally costs $19.99. As for the TV itself, it’s a 2026 model that sits below the U7SG (also on sale for $1,297.99, from $1,999.99) in Hisense's lineup as the brand's entry point into Mini LED, pairing a 4K panel and local dimming with a matte, anti-reflective coating meant to cut down on glare, notes this PCMag review.

For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. It also does a good job cleaning up lower-quality content, which is useful for older cable broadcasts or compressed YouTube videos—and its Fire TV interface makes it easy to jump between those kinds of content and the major streaming services without needing a separate streaming device.

The U6 Pro also brings plenty to the table for gaming, with HDMI 2.1, VRR, ALLM, and a 144Hz refresh rate that PC gamers can push to 240Hz at a lower 1080p resolution. That said, the panel’s slow response time and poor motion performance can reportedly make fast-moving scenes look noticeably blurry. Viewing angles are limited too, with the picture losing quality fairly quickly when you move off-center—and its built-in speakers aren’t particularly impressive either, so a soundbar could be worth budgeting for.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: Think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3396. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.
