#3379. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

#3377. 7 Prime Video Action Shows With No Bad Seasons, Ranked

Prime Video has a fantastic slate of originals. In fact, some of its newest shows have counted among the most talked about this year. And many of them fall into the action genre. From secret spies to law enforcement, military men and women, superheroes and super not-so-heroes, ghouls, and villains, the list is extensive, the shows filled with memorable characters.

Some shows waver and dip, losing their luster eventually and overstaying their welcome. But the best action shows on Prime Video don't have a single bad season among the bunch. Sure, two of them have only streamed one season so far. But these singular seasons were so incredibly entertaining, you won't be disappointed by watching them.

Not since Thelma & Louise have we had such a fun, female-centric buddy action adventure comedy like Ride or Die. Hannah Waddingham is a downright badass as elite assassin Judith Burton. She has hidden her identity from her best friend Deborah "Debbie" Claybourne (Octavia Spencer) since they became friends years prior. But current circumstances mean Debbie is in for a wild ride she never saw coming, and is going to be introduced to a side of her friend she didn't know existed.

The series, one of the best Prime Video shows in 2026 so far, is so fun throughout its eight episodes. It's as much a story of female friendship and dealing with childhood trauma as it is an action-packed show. But there are also fantastic fight sequences with engaging choreography, and intense physical and emotional moments. The fact that two female actors lead the story is refreshing. Sadly, Ride or Die was cancelled after its first season. But it's a fantastic weekend binge-watch with the gal pals or partner that provides a satisfying ending.

One of those enduring Prime Video shows that no one talks about, The Legend of Vox Machina has streamed four seasons already and will be coming back for a fifth and final season. The adult animated fantasy series based on the first Dungeons & Dragons campaign called Critical Role, follows a seven-member team embarking on a mission to avenge the murder of their town's rulers. The story develops from there in subsequent seasons as the characters grow and the battles evolve.

Initially, the series was funded through a Kickstarter campaign, yet it has since become one of Prime Video's most enduring originals. In her Season 4 review, Collider's Victoria Luxford says the show remains just as strong, a "funny, thrilling, and surprisingly deep fantasy series that balances fan service with a story that won't leave newcomers alienated." Once you have powered through The Legend of Vox Machina, check out its spin-off/sequel series The Mighty Nein.

One of the most polarizing shows of this decade, The Boys was set up to satirize the current political and societal landscape, and ended up becoming like a mirror of the times. The story in the satirical superhero series, a Prime Video show with no bad seasons, centers around an alternate world whereby humans live among those with superhuman abilities. Some of these powers are typical, like superhuman strength, speed, laser eyes, and invisibility. But others are more gruesome, vulgar, even offensive. And what these "Supes" do is nothing close to heroic: they're focused on feeding their egos and the pocketbook of the company that manages them, not actually helping others.

The Boys is subversive, politically commentative, and extremely violent. It isn't a show that everyone will like. But some will appreciate the deep meaning masked behind blood, gore, and a record number of male appendages and expletives. If you dig in to the root of the show, it's actually one of the smartest shows on television. Watch the entire five-season run and follow it up with the companion series Gen V.

I might be in the minority, but I actually like Neagley better than Reacher. Both shows are fantastic, but Neagley came out of the gate strong with its first season. And with a Season 2 renewal, it will likely get even better. The character of Frances Neagley (Maria Sten), who is first introduced in Reacher, is much more layered than Reacher fans realized. She shows up on that show as a trusted confidante, someone Jack Reacher (Alan Ritchson) knows he can count on to get the job done, no matter how challenging. He knows she will have his back and will always be two steps ahead, able to anticipate what he might need. This is emphasized in Neagley where Frances is clearly valued at the private investigation firm where she works. But she's also just as rebellious and against the rules as her friend Reacher is. The ensemble nature of the show introduces conflicting personalities that come together to form sort of a ragtag team.

The story in Season 1 follows Frances' investigation into the death of an old friend, which leads her to a dangerous cult and strange experiments. It has all the elements you'd expect from a good action crime show, including intense hunts, lots of engaging fight scenes, and emotional backstories that draw you into the characters themselves, not just the plot.

Having only just recently binged all of Reacher, the show's flow is still fresh in my mind. The later seasons are arguably better than the first two, but there still isn't a bad season among the bunch. Season 1 sets up Ritchson as the first actor to truly embody the character as he is in the Lee Child books. The stakes rise higher in Season 2, and the personal connection to the cases grows and becomes more intimate with each passing season.

The action and intensity is amped up in later seasons, too, with some of the most intriguing villains. The fact that the action crime drama has so much source material to work from with Child having written 31 novels about the character to date, there's no shortage of exciting stories from which to draw. If you love action shows, Reacher is among the best, with a protagonist who towers over his prey, doesn't flinch when he has to kill a bad guy, yet has the softest heart and strongest moral code. With at least two more seasons already confirmed, it's a good time to binge-watch the show and catch up on all the literal action.

Mark Grayson (Steven Yeun) just wants to be a regular teenager, but he doesn't have that chance. He's the son of the most powerful superhero on Earth, Omni-Man (J. K. Simmons), so he has a duty to serve. That means honing his skills now that he's coming of age and his latent powers are starting to show up. That's the set-up for the story in Invincible, an adult animated superhero series from Robert Kirkman that has become a huge pop culture phenomenon.

Even though it's animated, Invincible is very violent, gruesome, and graphic, so this isn't necessarily a show to watch with young kids. The stories are also quite mature. But the show is completely bingeable and addictive, adding depth to an otherwise thin story of good guys versus bad. Earning widespread acclaim, Invincible has already been renewed for two more seasons, continuing the story as Mark grapples with a shocking truth about his dad and fighting an evil group looking to conquer Earth.

The action doesn't start immediately in Fallout, but when it does, it happens in a big way. And the Prime Video show hooks you in the first five minutes. It begins with a betrayal in an underground bunker and expands to include the Earth above where there's nothing but conflict. Based on the video game franchise of the same name, Fallout follows Lucy (Ella Purnell) and her journey to find her kidnapped father, leaving the safety of her underground home for the first time. She comes across interesting and dangerous people, including The Ghoul (Walton Goggins), who has an interesting backstory and who is on a mission that eventually overlaps with Lucy's.

You'll see everything from Radroaches (giant, mutated cockroaches) attacking humans to robots, men in robotic armor, mutated creatures, undead ghouls, and a lot of eccentric personalities as people do whatever they can to survive in this post-apocalyptic world. The show wonderfully introduces new groups and characters each season while the journeys of Lucy and The Ghoul make progress and eventually come together. With only two seasons so far and a third on the way, considering there are five main video game stories and six spin-offs or mobile titles, there's lots more story to tell. If you like seeing unique fight scenes that you won't see in any other show, Fallout won't disappoint.

#3375. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3373. The Rings of Power’ Officially Confirms a Major Season 3 Storyline Was Scrapped Because of One Actor

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has plenty of logistical challenges to overcome, and fortunately, its cast seems to have a pretty good understanding of what's expected of them. However, not every actor is capable, and during production on the show's third season, one particularly troublesome performer managed to cause enough problems that the creative team had to rethink its plans.

Speaking exclusively with Maggie Lovitt for Collider Behind the Scenes, co-showrunner Patrick McKay and director Charlotte Brändström revealed that a dog introduced in Season 3 was originally supposed to have a much larger role, but to be blunt, he was not a very good boy. McKay told Collider:

"We had this idea that Arondir had a dog, and there's this scene — I actually really love this scene. I love the way you put it together — where Galadriel returns home from the battle, and everyone else has a partner or a child waiting for them. Even Arondir has the dog, and she has no one. I find it very touching, and I love Morfydd's performance. But the idea that this dog would be in many scenes and be a source of humor and interact with the Orc, and I think we even had an idea of bringing the dog back later in the season. No, that dog was an absolute nightmare."

Brändström admitted that the animal certainly looked the part, but getting it to behave long enough to film anything was another matter entirely. She explained, "He looked great. He looked how we wanted, but we managed to get him to eat the bone at some point. It was very hard to keep him still. It was very hard to keep him still long enough to say, 'Camera, start rolling.'" McKay then revealed just how much unusable footage the production accumulated while attempting to work with the animal. "There's a hard drive filled with, like, bum takes and the dog whimpering and yelling and barking and going after the Orc. I mean, it was a nightmare," McKay laughed. "So we ended up with less dog. However, I think that a little bit of dog goes a long way."

While the dog's intended recurring storyline was scaled back, its introduction is part of a much larger effort to make Middle-earth feel more tangible in Season 3. The new episodes introduce Rivendell, the famous Elven sanctuary that audiences will recognize from Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings movies. McKay told Collider:

"We really like building things. We really want these fantastical worlds to feel real and tangible and immersive. You know, one example I think of in the first episode is we introduce Rivendell, right? And I think the move that you and Alex came up with is starting in a virtual world and then entering into a physical set all in one shot. We do that a lot because one makes the other feel more real, right? And I think we're constantly looking for something photographic to ground it in."

Brändström agreed, emphasizing the importance of giving the actors something real to interact with, even when their surroundings will eventually be expanded digitally. "For the actors, it's important to feel grounded. They need to touch stuff. They need to feel the world around them," she explained. "They don't really care about whether we extend it then and add some mountains in the background, because they don't look at that. But they need to have something to be grounded, to touch, to feel. I mean, we even brought in horses on the stages and had a road that they could come up."

#3372. Netflix's One Piece Is Replacing Crocodile In Season 3

Warning! This article contains potential spoilers for Netflix's One Piece season 3 and major spoilers for the manga and anime.

As Crocodile steps into a bigger role in One Piece season 3, another villain is likely to make his presence known in the highly anticipated next installment of Netflix's hit fantasy show. Throughout the franchise, Crocodile has been one of One Piece's most beloved villains. Famous for his stylish look, signature facial scar, and golden hook hand, the fan-favorite antagonist is also a powerful Devil Fruit user who can manipulate sand.

In Netflix's One Piece, True Blood alum Joe Manganiello plays Crocodile. Season 2 introduced him as Mr. 0, the mysterious leader of the crime syndicate Baroque Works, who sent his agents after Princess Vivi and the Straw Hat Pirates. One Piece Season 2 ended with the reveal that Mr. 0 was actually Crocodile, a member of the World Government's Seven Warlords of the Sea. This title grants him immunity from the Marines. In exchange for being the World Government's ally, warlords can continue with their pirate activities.

With One Piece season 3 finally tackling the Alabasta arc, Crocodile will officially step out of the shadows to enact his plans to hijack the Alabasta Kingdom's throne from Vivi's father, King Cobra. While he becomes the new season's main villain, another popular antagonist will begin to cast an even bigger shadow over the entire narrative: Blackbeard. Unlike Crocodile, Blackbeard is poised to become the Straw Hat Pirates' most terrifying recurring threat in future seasons.

The audience will likely learn more about Blackbeard in One Piece season 3 through Portgas D. Ace's storyline. Luffy's brother Ace, portrayed by Cobra Kai star Xolo Maridueña, will finally be introduced during the Alabasta arc. While Ace's storyline involves him helping Luffy and the Straw Hats against the Marines and Baroque Works, it will also be revealed that he's on a mission to hunt down Blackbeard, who betrayed the Whitebeard Pirates after he murdered a fellow crew member to acquire the power of the Yami Yami no Mi, or Dark-Dark Fruit.

In Eiichiro Oda's long-running One Piece manga, Blackbeard, also known as Marshall D. Teach, originally served as a Whitebeard Pirate under Edward Newgate, one of the Four Emperors ruling the Grand Line. As one of Whitebeard's commanders, Ace took it upon himself to avenge his friend's death. However, Ace's Flame-Flame Fruit powers were no match for Blackbeard's dominant Devil Fruit power, which gives him the ability to consume everything into a black hole and nullify the Devil Fruit powers of anyone he touches.

Because of Blackbeard's overpowering Devil Fruit gift and manipulative strategy, Ace's unsanctioned solo revenge mission eventually leads to one of One Piece's most heartbreaking story arcs to date. Through Ace, Blackbeard gets closer to his ambitious goal, while also establishing himself as one of Luffy's most formidable enemies.

So far, Netflix hasn't announced any casting news for Blackbeard in One Piece season 3. However, given Blackbeard's importance to Ace's storyline, the show teasing his impending introduction in the new season wouldn't be surprising. As seen in the first two seasons, the live-action adaptation tends to reshuffle the manga's timeline to focus on major character introductions. Fan favorites like Monkey D. Garp, Bartolomeo, Sabo, and Brook have already appeared in the Netflix series, ahead of their official canon debuts. The writers could easily start laying the groundwork for Blackbeard's live-action arrival in the upcoming season.

Like Luffy, Blackbeard has also become one of the Four Emperors in the current storyline of the One Piece anime and manga. The live-action adaptation still has a long way to go before it can adapt their ascent in the New World era. However, Netflix's One Piece series can certainly plant the seeds for Luffy and Blackbeard's parallel rise to power and inevitable rivalry. Instead of the all-powerful ruler Imu, Blackbeard could become the final obstacle in Luffy's journey to finding the One Piece and becoming King of Pirates.

Making Blackbeard the ultimate endgame villain of One Piece would be more meaningful than having Luffy face an ancient god like Imu because of the years-long build-up that's tied their journeys together. Luffy and Blackbeard are ideological mirrors of one another, sharing many similarities from their unwavering belief in dreams to having the mysterious "Will of D," to their ambitious goal of claiming the One Piece. Despite this, they use opposing methods to achieve their dreams. Luffy appreciates loyalty, camaraderie, and freedom, while Blackbeard attains his goal through chaos and domination.

One Piece season 3 arrives on Netflix in 2027.

#3369. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3368. 'The Martian' Meets 'Interstellar' in Netflix's 10-Episode Sci-Fi Drama Made for Your Next Binge

Amanda M. Castro is a Network TV writer at Collider and a New York–based journalist whose work has appeared in Newsweek, where she is an Associate Editor, and The U.S. Sun, where she previously served as a Senior Consumer Reporter.

She specializes in network television coverage, delivering sharp, thoughtful analysis of long-running procedural hits and ambitious new dramas across broadcast TV. At Collider, Amanda explores character arcs, storytelling trends, and the cultural impact of network series that keep audiences tuning in week after week.

Born and raised in Puerto Rico, Amanda is bilingual and holds a degree in Communication, Film, and Media Studies from the University of New Haven.

Getting to Mars is hard enough, but leaving everyone you love behind might be even harder. Netflix's Away takes the idea of a mission to the Red Planet and fleshes it out on a more personal level by following a crew of astronauts as they try to make history while managing their relationships and obligations at home. The 10-episode science-fiction series, which stars two-time Oscar winner Hilary Swank, will likely appeal to fans of The Martian's survival aspect and Interstellar's family-oriented storytelling. Plenty of complications arise aboard the spacecraft, but some of the show's hardest moments happen millions of miles away.

Created by Andrew Hinderaker, Away premiered on Netflix in September 2020. Although the series was canceled after its first season, its 10 episodes tell a largely self-contained story about the first crewed mission to Mars. The journey takes three years, and the people aboard have much to lose before they reach their destination, making for a different kind of space drama that draws as much interest from people watching from Earth as from the astronauts traveling through space.

Swank stars as Emma Green, a NASA astronaut selected to command the Atlas, a spacecraft carrying an international crew on humanity's first mission to Mars. Joining her are Indian pilot and medical officer Ram Arya (Ray Panthaki), Chinese chemist Lu Wang (Vivian Wu), Russian cosmonaut Misha Popov (Mark Ivanir), and British botanist Kwesi Weisberg-Abban (Ato Essandoh). They come from different backgrounds and have varying levels of experience, but they share the significant responsibility of getting to Mars alive.

Emma's appointment as commander is hardly straightforward, as some crew members question her leadership after an early emergency aboard the Atlas, leaving her to earn their confidence while managing the demands of an increasingly dangerous expedition. They also face the challenge of keeping everyone alive for three years in a confined spacecraft. Equipment malfunctions, medical emergencies, and problems with the ship's essential systems put the mission at risk, forcing the astronauts to rely on one another even when their personal differences get in the way.

One of the mission's most compelling aspects is its international nature. Every astronaut goes through a unique set of experiences that influence their relationships throughout the mission. Misha is a seasoned space traveler, with a lot of turbulence in his personal life as the price of his success. Kwesi is a newcomer to astronautics, with knowledge of botany and some faith beliefs that influence how he sees the mission.

Although this book has a central theme of the technological obstacles of space travel, much of the content focuses on events on Earth. Here, Matt Logan (Josh Charles), Emma's husband, and their daughter, Alexis “Lex” Logan (Talitha Bateman), must learn to cope without Emma. Matt is an ex-astronaut who was unable to join the expedition due to his medical problems and suffered a stroke shortly after Emma's departure. As a result, the family faces issues beyond the distance between Earth and Mars. Recovery includes both the difficult rehabilitation process for Matt while Lex is doing everything in her power to deal with the experiences of being a mother without her mother and caring for her father. All Emma can do is accept that, unfortunately, she cannot simply abandon the mission every time something goes wrong at home.

Christopher Nolan's Interstellar explores the emotional consequences of space exploration through a father and daughter separated by an extraordinary journey. Away approaches a similar idea from a different family dynamic, with a mother attempting to reconcile her professional ambitions with her responsibilities as a parent. The separation is difficult for everyone involved, and the series gives those feelings considerable room to develop.

Of course, viewers looking for the relentless action of The Martian should adjust their expectations. Away has its share of emergencies, including a damaged solar panel and a failing water reclamation system, but it often prioritizes the crew's emotional lives over the mechanics of survival. That's a deliberate choice, although it occasionally comes at the expense of the show's pacing.

One thing prospective viewers should know before settling in for all 10 episodes is that Away will not return for Season 2; Netflix canceled the series in October 2020, just weeks after its premiere. The decision was reportedly tied to production costs, with individual episodes costing about $6 million, despite the show's early streaming success.

The good news is that the first season does give a certain amount of closure. The Atlas arrives at Mars, and the crew manages to pull through with the main mission goals. Although some characters have unresolved issues and contradictions that could be developed in the second season, they still get enough closure related to the mission itself.

For anyone who is interested in a show about astronauts who spend as much time thinking about their loved ones as performing operations in outer space, Away is unsurprisingly worth watching. The show may struggle with pacing and its emotional core, and some of the emotional backstory may feel too sweet. Nevertheless, Swank and the other actors give the series a personality you can't help but appreciate.

The stop-motion episodes tell more stories for Huntrix and The Saja Boys from behind the scenes, and it's now available to stream on Netflix.

On top of that, Netflix also released a three-episode mini-series titled KPop Toy Creations, which comprises mini episodes inspired by the film, and also a four-episode Play Games with Us series, which is also stop-motion and includes competitions and challenges inspired by the original film. It’s widely expected that Netflix and Sony will release shorter-form spinoffs of KPop Demon Hunters before the sequel arrives, with major clamor from the fans to see some Derpy and Sussie stories at the very least. That expectation was somewhat set by the apparent reveal of short film, Debut: A KPop Demon Hunters Story, back in September 2025, for which an MPA Classification and Rating Administration filing appeared.

Speculation suggests Debut will be an origin story revealing how the band came together, thanks to the title, but little is actually known. So far, a release date hasn’t been revealed, with Netflix typically keeping that information locked down.

If you haven't already, you can pick up iconic looks inspired by Huntrix and The Saja Boys, both in terms of their everyday style stage outfits that can be mixed for personalization. There's also a new in-game music player that includes four of the movie's original songs - “Golden,” “How It’s Done,” “Soda Pop” and “Your Idol" - which can be used as players' own soundtracks up until November 23.

So far, we've only had one LEGO set for KPop Demon Hunters with the Derpy and Sussie set that landed on shelves back in August, but the original announcement came with a promise of 2027 sets. Leaks posted by BrickFanatics suggest fans can expect five KPop Demon Hunters LEGO sets and a polybag release on May 1, 2027, ranging from $24.99 up to $129.99. There are other 2027 books coming for KPop Demon Hunter fans, including KPop Demon Hunters: Official How to Draw Netflix KPop Demon Hunters, which is set for March, and KPop Demon Hunters: Official Paper Dolly Dress-up Book, coming in April. Neither really expands the franchise in any way, but nice to have for fans.

The game will be playable by two to six players over a 60-minute session and uses lightweight motion-tracking headsets, projection mapping, and touch-sensitive walls. Players will be able to create their own animated avatar, joining Huntrix to protect the Honmoon through a series of mini games. Tickets start at $39, while the VIP Package, priced at $99, includes all-day access to the VIP Lounge, including complimentary snacks and refreshments and a choice of a VIP-exclusive tote or plush bag clip, as long as supplies last.

In what will surely be a major revenue driver, Netflix and AEG Presents have announced that a KPop Demon Hunters world tour is on the way. Tour locations have not yet been announced, but it’s expected to kick off in 2027, with 150 stops across the world. You can sign up for more information here.

Either way, it’s going to pull in a lot of families. #3366. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

The new artwork was announced by the official Jujutsu Kaisen anime account and Anime Updates for Jump Festa 2027. Its cheer squad theme features five full-length portraits in separate colored frames. Kinji Hakari appears against yellow, Kirara Hoshi gets pink, Yuji is framed in orange, Megumi in teal, and Yuta in blue.

#3361. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The company introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen shows that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That said, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3359. The 6 Most Hopeless HBO Shows, Ranked

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

A hopeless HBO show is usually about crime happening, and audience rooting for the criminal. You immediately know this is going to be good but with a guilt. Someone finally gets out. That's usually when I start worrying. They've survived the murderers, escaped the prison, defeated the enemy, or found the person they've spent years searching for. Surely they deserve one peaceful morning. But HBO has made an entire art form out of asking what happens after survival.

Sometimes the answer is so cruel that I wish the character had never started hoping in the first place. And I'm an absolute sucker for these stories. I get attached to people who make awful decisions, defend characters who probably deserve criticism, and celebrate tiny victories as though they've personally changed my life. These six shows have given me plenty of reasons to believe things might improve. That's what makes watching those hopes collapse so bloody painful.

Nobody understands the cruelty of Westeros quite like the Stark family. Ned Stark (Sean Bean) arrives in King's Landing believing that honor and duty still mean something, only to discover that the political world surrounding the Iron Throne operates according to considerably uglier rules. Game of Thrones follows the violent struggle between noble houses as betrayals, wars, and supernatural threats destroy entire families. What begins with one honorable man's attempt to uncover a conspiracy becomes a continent-wide tragedy.

And I still haven't forgiven this show for Shireen Baratheon (Kerry Ingram). She's a gentle, intelligent child who loves reading and offers kindness to Ser Davos (Liam Cunningham), one of the few adults who treats her with genuine affection. Then her father Stannis (Stephen Dillane) permits her sacrifice in a desperate attempt to improve his military fortunes. Watching Davos discover what happened is devastating. Shireen did nothing to deserve that fate. Her death doesn't even secure the victory Stannis wanted. That's Westeros at its most merciless. Innocence offers no protection, and enormous suffering can accomplish absolutely nothing.

Christopher Moltisanti (Michael Imperioli) wants to become a respected gangster, build a career in Hollywood, and enjoy a future with Adriana La Cerva (Drea de Matteo). Unfortunately, he's devoted his life to Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini), a New Jersey mob boss whose affection often comes with terrifying conditions. The Sopranos follows Tony's criminal empire and troubled family life, exposing how greed, insecurity, and violence gradually poison practically every relationship around him.

The moment Christopher chooses Tony over Adriana still makes me furious. She's been cooperating with the FBI and finally tells Christopher the truth, hoping they can escape together. He initially appears willing. Then he sees a miserable-looking family at a gas station and decides against abandoning his comfortable criminal life. Adriana pays for that decision with her life. And Christopher eventually dies at Tony's own hands. That's the terrible logic running through David Chase's masterpiece. These people repeatedly recognize the possibility of changing their lives, then retreat into the very behavior destroying them. Tony attends therapy for years. He can articulate his unhappiness beautifully. Somehow, that rarely makes him kinder.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

Joel (Pedro Pascal) has already endured the death of his daughter when he's entrusted with escorting Ellie (Bella Ramsey) across an America devastated by a fungal pandemic. Ellie may be humanity's best hope of developing a cure, but their dangerous journey gradually turns two lonely survivors into something resembling a family. The Last of Us builds its emotional foundation around that relationship, then confronts them with the terrible consequences of Joel's determination to protect her.

There's a birthday when Joel takes Ellie to an abandoned museum, places an astronaut helmet on her head, and plays a recording of a rocket launch. For a few minutes, she's simply a happy child imagining space. God, I love that moment. Then I remember their later conversation on the porch, where Joel finally admits what he did to save her from the Fireflies. Ellie tells him she wants to try forgiving him. That possibility is painfully precious because we know how little time they have left. Her subsequent pursuit of revenge only spreads the suffering to more people. This world can take practically everything from someone, then turn their love for the dead into another source of destruction.

Nora Durst (Carrie Coon) loses her husband and two children in an instant. They simply vanish, along with two percent of the world's population, leaving everybody else without an explanation. The Leftovers begins three years after that event, following people who have developed increasingly desperate ways of coping with an absence nobody can understand. Police chief Kevin Garvey (Justin Theroux) struggles with his own psychological turmoil, while religious movements emerge around competing interpretations of what happened.

Nora breaks my heart because she cannot even mourn in a way people recognize. There are no bodies to bury, no confirmed deaths, and no reason she can accept for why her family disappeared while she remained. Her suffering becomes something strangers are fascinated by, although their curiosity offers her nothing. Then the series introduces the possibility of sending people wherever the departed went, and Nora must decide whether to risk everything for an answer. Damon Lindelof and Tom Perrotta created this drama.

Baltimore's police officers, drug dealers, politicians, teachers, and working families inhabit the same city while experiencing completely different versions of it. The Wire begins with a criminal investigation led by detective Jimmy McNulty (Dominic West) before expanding into an extraordinary portrait of institutions that repeatedly fail the people depending on them. The tragedy isn't simply that bad things happen. It's that the machinery responsible for preventing those things often helps them continue.

Bodie Broadus (J. D. Williams) is the character I keep returning to. He starts as a young drug dealer working for Avon Barksdale's organization and spends years surviving changes in leadership, violence, and constant threats to his position. Eventually, he recognizes how little his loyalty has earned him. Yet when Marlo Stanfield's men come to kill him, Bodie refuses to abandon his corner. He dies defending a tiny patch of Baltimore that never offered him anything resembling a future. That image is almost unbearable.

Emerald City sounds like somewhere people might find a fresh start. Instead, it's an experimental unit inside Oswald State Correctional Facility, where inmates are supposedly given a better chance at rehabilitation. Oz quickly destroys that promise. Tobias Beecher (Lee Tergesen), a lawyer imprisoned after killing a child while driving drunk, enters expecting punishment and encounters a world where humiliation, violence, and exploitation become everyday realities. Tom Fontana, who created the series, makes the prison's supposedly progressive ambitions feel like a particularly cruel joke. People enter hoping to serve their sentences and eventually leave. Some barely survive their first week.

But Cyril O'Reily (Scott William Winters) is the character whose suffering I find hardest to accept. Living with a brain injury and dependent on his manipulative brother Ryan (Dean Winters), Cyril is drawn into murder and eventually faces execution. Watching Ryan desperately try to save the one person who loves him unconditionally is devastating, especially knowing how much suffering Ryan himself has caused. And that's the horrible thing about Oz. It doesn't ask us to pretend these prisoners are innocent. It makes us recognize their humanity even after confronting their worst actions. Beecher becomes increasingly brutal just to survive. Cyril never fully understands the machinery determining his fate. The institution promises justice but repeatedly manufactures more suffering. I've watched countless television characters lose everything. Few have frightened me like the men of Oz, because even surviving their punishment can mean losing whatever remains of themselves.

#3358. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3357. NBC Breaks SNL's 52-Season Rule For An Undeniable Industry Shift

For more than five decades, Saturday Night Live has relied on some of entertainment's biggest names to attract audiences. From Hollywood actors and chart-topping musicians to professional athletes, NBC's long-running sketch comedy series has traditionally featured hosts whose careers were established through mainstream entertainment.

However, as the industry continues to evolve, SNL is beginning to recognize that celebrity status is considerably different from what it once was. Social media has fundamentally changed how audiences discover and engage with entertainers, creating an entirely new generation of celebrities whose influence rivals that of established Hollywood stars.

Platforms like YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram have become launching pads for successful entertainment careers. Despite the growing popularity of digital content creators, Saturday Night Live has largely maintained its traditional approach to selecting hosts throughout its impressive 52-season run. That changed on November 7, 2026, when comedian and content creator Druski became the first digital-native influencer to host the series.

While his appearance was already a significant milestone for Saturday Night Live, the episode's remarkable ratings proved just how valuable internet personalities could become to traditional television. More importantly, Druski's success could fundamentally change how NBC approaches the show's future, potentially opening the door for an entirely new generation of hosts.

Throughout Saturday Night Live's 52-season history, the show has typically reserved its hosting opportunities for established figures in entertainment. Actors frequently appear to promote upcoming films or television projects, musicians use the platform to reach new audiences, and professional athletes occasionally step outside their comfort zones to demonstrate their comedic abilities. Even the show's stand-up comedian hosts generally arrive with careers built through traditional comedy clubs, television appearances, or major comedy specials.

Importantly, SNL has previously embraced performers who developed followings online, including several of its own cast members. However, those opportunities typically involved bringing digital talent into the show's established ensemble rather than handing an internet personality the responsibility of hosting an entire episode. Druski's appearance marked the first time a digital-native creator received that distinction, demonstrating NBC's willingness to reconsider what qualifies someone for the coveted hosting opportunity.

Found an error? Send it info@screenrant.com so it can be corrected.

The decision also reflects how dramatically the entertainment industry's definition of celebrity has changed. Druski did not need a breakout movie role or a successful network sitcom to become recognizable to millions of viewers. Instead, he built his audience independently, proving that digital creators can establish the kind of cultural relevance traditionally associated with Hollywood stars. By welcoming him to Studio 8H, Saturday Night Live acknowledged that its next generation of influential hosts might emerge from platforms that didn't exist when the series first premiered.

Druski's Saturday Night Live debut was more than a historic first for the NBC comedy series. It was also an undeniable ratings success, suggesting that embracing digital content creators could be an effective strategy for attracting new audiences. According to Nielsen's Live+Same Day figures, the November 7 episode attracted approximately 5.6 million television viewers, making it the show's most-watched broadcast in two years. This represented an 8% increase over the previous week's episode, hosted by Inde Navarrette, which had already established a season 52 high.

Perhaps more importantly, Druski's appearance delivered impressive results among younger viewers. The episode attracted an estimated 1.5 million adults aged 18–49, an 18% increase over the previous week. It also earned SNL its strongest performance among viewers aged 18–34 in more than four years (via USA Today). These demographics are particularly significant because they demonstrate the show's ability to attract audiences who increasingly consume entertainment through digital platforms rather than traditional television.

The success extended beyond NBC's linear broadcast. Druski's episode became the most-watched Saturday Night Live installment in Peacock's history (via The Wrap), although the streaming service has not released its exact audience figures. Meanwhile, clips from the episode generated an astonishing 424 million views across YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, and X within three days. While these social media figures count video plays rather than individual viewers, they demonstrate the extraordinary reach that an internet personality can bring to an established television institution.

Of course, Druski cannot receive all the credit for these numbers. The episode benefited from a strong college football lead-in, musical guest The Strokes, and several high-profile appearances. Nevertheless, the combination of traditional television success, record-breaking streaming performance, and widespread social media engagement gives NBC a compelling reason to reconsider its hosting strategy. Rather than treating Druski's appearance as an isolated experiment, SNL could begin regularly welcoming digital creators whose established audiences offer opportunities for continued growth.

Although Druski's established following undoubtedly contributed to his Saturday Night Live debut's success, the episode also demonstrated why his particular brand of comedy translates so well to television. Rather than forcing the internet personality to abandon the exaggerated characters and absurd situations that made him famous, SNL embraced those strengths. The result was an episode that balanced the show's familiar sketch comedy format with the unpredictable humor audiences already associate with Druski.

His opening monologue established that approach immediately. Druski enthusiastically celebrated the opportunity while joking about the restrictions placed on his performance, including his inability to promise that he wouldn't violate the show's rules. The monologue also featured a surprise appearance from Emma Stone, his co-star in the upcoming film The Catch. Although the segment was relatively brief, it allowed Druski to introduce himself to unfamiliar viewers without sacrificing the humor that made him popular online.

Saturday Night Live's best guest hosts bring their own unique energy to the show while fitting neatly into the sketch show's goofy sense of humor.

Several sketches played directly into his comedic strengths. In "Dru Can See Everything," Druski parodied disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, leaning into the elaborate physical transformations that have become a defining feature of his online videos. Meanwhile, "Birthday Girl" featured him portraying an excessively demanding birthday celebrant, while "Bubu Mobile" paired him with Marcello Hernández as employees at a Dominican phone store. These performances showcased his ability to create distinctive characters while working alongside the established SNL ensemble.

However, Druski wasn't the episode's only attraction. Its political cold open featured an unexpected appearance from Texas Senator-elect James Talarico, while Weekend Update addressed the aftermath of the midterm elections. Musical guest The Strokes also delivered two performances, adding another recognizable name to the broadcast. Combined with Druski's enthusiastic hosting performance, these elements helped make the episode appealing to viewers beyond his existing fanbase.

Ultimately, the episode's popularity suggests SNL does not need to reinvent itself to accommodate digital creators. Druski succeeded by bringing his established comedic identity into the show's existing format, demonstrating how both sides could benefit from the collaboration. If NBC wants to replicate that success, embracing more internet personalities could be vital for keeping Saturday Night Live culturally relevant for another generation.

Saturday Night Live airs Saturdays at 11:30 EDT on NBC.

Saturday Night Live is a live television sketch comedy and variety show created by Lorne Michaels, premiering in 1975. It features comedy sketches parodying contemporary culture and politics, performed by a rotating cast. Each episode is hosted by a celebrity guest and includes musical performances.
