#3356. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3355. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3354. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3353. ‘Rivals’ Aidan Turner and Victoria Smurfit Breaks Down Season 2's Most Vicious Fight

Greer Riddell is a London-based film and television journalist writing about comedy, streaming and the evolving media industry in the UK and USA. She works at Collider, covering the latest in film, television and entertainment through interviews, features, reviews and industry coverage.

Her recent brand collaborations include HBO, Warner Bros., Netflix, Hulu, Sky, Disney+ and DC Studios. She has covered titles including Saturday Night Live UK, Rivals, Scrubs, Stuart Fails to Save the Universe, Ludwig, Supergirl and Stranger Things.

Her recent interviews include Florence Pugh, Mike Faist and Christopher Abbott for Netflix's East of Eden, Taika Waititi and Jenna Ortega for Klara and the Sun.

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for Rivals Season 2, Episodes 7-9.It's been a long wait since June to find out whether Tony Baddingham (David Tennant) and Maud O'Hara (Victoria Smurfit) will get their comeuppance after their affair led to Monica Baddingham (Claire Rushbrook) dying in a car accident during a storm. Rivals is never short of drama, and that's not all for the Baddinghams, as it was revealed earlier in the season that Sarah Stratton's (Emily Atack) baby is also Tony's illegitimate child.

To explore these cliffhangers and more, Collider joined Aidan Turner, Smurfit, and Atack to discuss the first three explosive episodes of Rivals Season 2, Part 2. They break down Declan and Maud's extraordinary argument on Bonfire Night and reveal whether Declan will finally give in to the urges he's been repressing out of fierce loyalty to his wife. Atack shares why she enjoys playing Sarah at her most vulnerable and why the most confident characters are often not what they seem. The trio also reveal what goes on behind the scenes on the Rivals set and whether being part of a series that's so much fun to watch is equally enjoyable to film.

COLLIDER: Well, I didn't think Rivals could get more dramatic, but the last three episodes, they've really blown it out of the water. And I have to ask first: that big showdown between Maud and Declan. Have you recovered from that? In the kitchen?

SMURFIT: I was just saying my hips are still sore!

TURNER: [Laughter] I feel really bad about that.

TURNER: Well, I kept on hitting the dirt.

SMURFIT: It's only a hairy second, isn't it?

TURNER: I kept throwing you down quite hard. It’s one of those ones...

TURNER: It's a year ago now; it still hurts.

SMURFIT: She does. Anyway, so yes, it was great. It was weirdly fun to do because it was such a juicy, beautifully written scene. So, it was like all the emotions, all the justifications, all the failings, all the passion, all... you know, it was just, oh, it was just juicy, wasn't it?

SMURFIT: You don't get many of those in your career.

TURNER: You don't. It's also, not that this should really matter — but it kind of does for me — it was a night shoot, and there's something that happens at nighttime. I find when I work, it just all goes a bit weird, and there was a strange energy in the air, and I kind of went wild. Maybe it was a full moon or something, but I felt a bit crazed that night. Did you?

SMURFIT: Well, yeah. You kept feckin’ me in a fire!

Is that something that you do as an actor to get yourself into that sort of big emotional state? Because you're really asked to go from zero to 11 in a really quick space of time.

TURNER: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, you just kind of do it, but it's also like, you want to stay present. Sometimes I think we split the scene where he runs out, but you're in the moment from moment to moment. So you can't play what's ahead of you.

SMURFIT: When you know where you're starting and the stuff that's behind you, you don't think about what's coming. You know where you're at, and then you put your foot on the gas, and you're playing with great actors, then it's all just sort of there.

There's a few moments, actually, in that where Declan was stood in the trees and him obviously being incredibly angry there. There were times where it was quite similar to the visuals we got of Tony and him being really angry. So I wondered if that was a conscious decision, or you thought about, actually, is Declan going to get to that Tony level of anger throughout?

TURNER: He did get really angry. I think he completely lost control.

TURNER: I was just saying earlier, I mean, which I sort of forgotten about, but I feel thankful there were other people around. I feel really scared when I think of what he would have done had no one else been there to stop him. It was a kind of blind anger he had.

I'm looking forward to seeing what happens when Sarah's secret fully comes out because it's been teased. A few people know. But when Tony actually finds out that has gone around the whole village, that's going to be mad. That's going to be another confrontation, I think! But I wanted to ask you, what's something you enjoy the most? Is it playing somebody who's really confident or at their most exposed? Because there are a lot of scenes in this where you're having some quite emotional moments.

ATACK: Yeah, I was really grateful for that. And I think what it touches on is the obvious thing that so many outwardly confident people are often inside, kind of, battling something else, battling vulnerability. And, yeah, women like Sarah are definitely that. I think she's learned to be a certain way. She has to be a certain way to survive in the world that she's in. You know, a male-dominated world, the world of telly.

I think that what's so great about the writing is characters like Sarah, who would have been so unlikable in other TV shows, but there's something about this. There's something about Rivals where you really root for people that are making all these terrible mistakes and making all these mental decisions.

I was really happy when I read the script that we got to expose that vulnerability underneath all the hair and the makeup and the confidence and sexiness. Because that's kind of true to life, really. Not me, just [laughs] confident people; they're often covering something.

The two stars of the Hulu series also break down their characters' toxic relationship.

So now that Declan has found out that Maud and Tony have been an item, he has obviously been very loyal to Maud before. Does this mean he might have a change of heart? May he explore seeing if Cameron's still interested? Is he going to explore some of those urges?

TURNER: I don't know what urges he's going to explore, but I think it's going to be difficult for him to come to terms with this. I think she hurt him in the most fundamental... I think it's been really hard on him, and that's going to continue. There's obviously so much love there, and they have this really strong connection, and there's been things in the past — different infidelities and affairs that they've managed to wade through, but this feels different this time. So, I don't know how it's going to play out. I don't know if he's going to be able to forgive. Maybe he will. I don't know.

Is there a behind-the-scenes moment for you that really sums up what it's like to have been a part of that set? Because it looks really fun from where we're watching at home.

SMURFIT: I think a lot of the memories, when we do... in a lot of the episodes, we have a set piece, as we call it, which is most of the cast all together at a Hunt Ball, at the polo, you know, all these different set pieces. And it's usually got an incredible story. Everyone's together, so they'll pull this group of people in, and the rest are held in the tent or in a room, and invariably what's happening is games of chess, games of cards, games of— what was that spy game that Brendan Patricks always brings?

SMURFIT: Codenames, where you're — it's basically like The Traitors — all lying. And, and so there are all these tables full of different, different actors sitting together playing the games. And it's so fun to watch everybody dip into the game; they're called, they go off to work, and then just somebody else will take over the game that they're playing. And it's like a big, weird family, dysfunctional children, and absolutely no adults.

You just made me think, actually, that all of the characters in Rivals, they'd be too good at playing The Traitors because they'd all be good at lying, and no one would be able to identify them.

ATACK: It's kind of like they are playing The Traitors!

TURNER: I don’t know if Declan would be very good at lying. Maybe not him, but, yeah, everyone else, maybe!

#3351. Former Police Officer to Be Castrated After Child Rape Conviction in Louisiana

Louisiana doesn't mess around when it comes to sex offenders ... a district judge has ordered a child rapist to be chemically castrated!

The rapist -- identified as 31-year-old Kedreyon K. Williams -- was convicted by a trial jury of rape of juveniles, indecent behavior with a juvenile, and possession of pornography involving juveniles. The jury took just 30 minutes to find Williams -- a former cop and volunteer firefighter -- guilty on all counts.

Because Williams was convicted of rape, prosecutors argued that he should face a mandatory life sentence and be physically castrated.

Tony Clayton — Louisiana's 18th Judicial District Attorney — called Williams a "child predator" who deserves to be chemically castrated as "another layer of punishment for these horrendous crimes."

Clayton added ... "If a man takes sexual advantage of a child, then we will take his manhood!"

At sentencing, District Judge Kevin Kimball agreed with Clayton and ordered the castration, saying Williams committed the worst case of child rape he's ever seen. Kimball also sentenced Williams to life in prison.

Under Louisiana’s castration law established in 2008, anyone convicted of a serious sex crime is subject to chemical or surgical castration by order of the case judge. In 2014, the law was amended, giving judges the option to order surgical castration for offenders convicted of abusing victims under the age of 13.

#3350. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

#3348. Everything You Should Know About Black Friday 2026 Sales: Early Deals, Dates, and Retailers

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales appear to be becoming a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. Now you can open your library when the clock strikes midnight in New Zealand on November 19, which is around 5am CT in the United States on November 18, and check if GTA 6 is available to play. #3345. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

#3343. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.

#3340. The Greatest Led Zeppelin Lyrics Ever Written, Ranked

Led Zeppelin is one of the biggest rock bands of all time. The group has its genesis in London, 1968, taking form after the dissolution of The Yardbirds – a blues-rock band that launched the careers of multiple legendary guitarists, Jimmy Page included. Zeppelin quickly rose to fame. Boasting eight consecutive number one albums in the UK and a 1995 induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (amongst many other accolades), their work has been appreciated and celebrated for decades.

Led Zeppelin's music is rooted in the blues and influenced by the British and American folk revival, giving their work immense depth and a unique texture. Their lyrics tackle all aspects of the human experience, from love and desire to the seemingly endless search for purpose. Emotional and introspective, frontman Robert Plant’s vivid storytelling played a key role in their massive success. While they have countless unforgettable lyrics, these five Led Zeppelin songs contain their very best.

“Over the Hills and Far Away” was written by Robert Plant and Jimmy Page during their time at Bron-Yr-Aur, a remote holiday cottage in Wales. After their North American tour wrapped, Plant and Page retreated to this peaceful oasis to recover, spend time in nature, and write. The cottage had no electricity or running water, so the pair spent many a cold evening making music by the roaring fire. This return to simplicity allowed them to create many beautiful pieces – the influence of the Welsh countryside can be heard throughout their discography.

“Over the Hills and Far Away,” the lead single from their 1973 album Houses of the Holy, is heavily influenced by Celtic folklore and Welsh mythology. The song’s title is a classic idiom from 17th century British folklore, referring to the romantic uncertainty of the future. It has a recurring role in English folk culture, a tradition that Zeppelin continued some 300 years later.

This song explores the ongoing search for purpose – the seemingly endless journey one must undertake in order to let go of the past and build the future. It is about breaking free, hitting the open road and living beyond the constraints of society. Most of all, it is about finding love. Plant writes about the toxic relationships of the past and dreams of a better future: “Many have I loved, and many times been bitten/ Many times I've gazed along the open road.” The cure for a broken heart? Adventure.

“Ramble On” is the seventh track on Led Zeppelin II, released in 1969. This song was heavily influenced by The Lord of the Rings trilogy, written by J.R.R. Tolkien. Tolkien and Page grew up in the same region in the West Midlands of England. Plant felt very connected to Tolkien and his literature, specifically his creation of Middle Earth, a fantasy land that romanticized the English countryside. This song directly references Tolkien characters and locales: “T'was in the darkest depths of Mordor/ I met a girl so fair/ But Gollum and the evil one/ Crept up and slipped away with her.”

This song follows the same classic monomyth structure as LOTR and The Hobbit – the main character must leave the comforts of home behind and journey into the unknown, a transformative experience necessary for personal growth. In Plant’s lyrics, this takes the form of leaving the fast-paced toxicity of urban living and returning to the natural world in order to find himself. His expedition is set up in the first verse: “The leaves are falling all around/ Time I was on my way/ Thanks to you, I'm much obliged/ For such a pleasant stay/ But now it's time for me to go/ The autumn moon lights my way/ For now, I smell the rain/ And with it pain/ And it's headed my way.”

“Stairway to Heaven” is widely regarded as one of the best rock songs of all time. It was also created during their stay at Bron-Yr-Aur, written mostly in a single night and then fleshed out through fragmented recordings. Plant initially improvised the lyrics on the spot, then refined them over time. This powerful progressive rock anthem is expansive and soaring, steeped in haunting folk magic.

The lyrics condemn the material greed and consumerism of the modern world. Plant ruminates upon society’s obsession with money: “There's a lady who's sure all that glitters is gold/ And she's buying a stairway to Heaven/ When she gets there she knows, if the stores are all closed/ With a word she can get what she came for.” Like much of his writing, the focus is on finding meaning in a seemingly meaningless existence. While he might not have all the answers, he knows that salvation and peace cannot be achieved through the accumulation of material things. The gently and poetically urges the listener to let go of ego and think beyond the self, to return to nature and discover inner peace. This song is Led Zeppelin’s pièce de résistance, and rightfully so.

You won't find "Stairway to Heaven" or "Kasmir" on this list.

“Kashmir” is perhaps the only other Zeppelin song in the same league (and on the same scale) as "Stairway." Plant was inspired not by the Indian region of Kashmir (as the title suggests), but instead by the vast emptiness of the deserts of Morocco: “Oh, all I see turns to brown/ As the sun burns the ground/ And my eyes fill with sand/ As I scan this wasted land/ Trying to find, trying to find where I've been.” The lyrics ruminate on the significance of the journey rather than the destination – the transformation itself is what is important, not the end result.

Every member of the band has songwriting credits on this track – except for multi-instrumentalist John Paul Jones, who was late for the recording session on the day it was written. Zeppelin considered this song one of their biggest musical accomplishments, often wishing they were known for “Kashmir” instead of “Stairway.” They performed constantly, gracing countless crowds with its magic and majesty. Plant is very proud of the lyrics, and deservedly so. His writing is abstract and poetic, capturing massive ideas and emotions in a handful of words: “Oh, let the sun beat down upon my face/ With stars to fill my dream/ I am a traveler of both time and space/ To be where I have been.”

Plant was only 22 when he wrote “Going to California.” The song is a lilting, melodic reflection upon the counterculture of the 1960s and the glamorization of the American West Coast. The track was initially about the earthquakes in California, which is still a theme in the lyrics: “Seems that the wrath of the Gods/ Got a punch on the nose and it started to flow/ I think I might be sinking.” As they worked on the song, earthquakes took on a metaphoric role: representing radical, transformative change in one’s life.

In continuity with much of his other work, the lyrics describe a search for a meaning through adventure and new experiences. Plant describes letting go of the toxicity of the past and the women who have scorned him: “Spent my days with a woman unkind/ Smoked my stuff and drank all my wine./ Made up my mind to make a new start/ Going To California with an aching in my heart.” California is framed as this fantasy world where anything is possible.

Plant describes the woman of his dreams: “To find a queen without a king/ They say she plays guitar and cries and sings/ Side a white mare in the footsteps of dawn/ Tryin' to find a woman who's never, never, never been born.” Plant has said that he finds these lyrics somewhat embarrassing in retrospect, but they captured how he was feeling at the time – which is exactly what songwriting should do. Some have posited that this mystical figure is inspired by Joni Mitchell, which may very well be the case. But more than anything, this song is a life-affirming love letter to California.

#3338. 10 Best Shows Like The Mentalist On Netflix

One of the best procedural dramas of the 2010s is The Mentalist, which introduced the audience to Patrick Jane (Simon Baker), and for those looking for something similar to it, Netflix has some excellent options. Procedural drama is a popular genre on TV, bringing some of the best TV shows of all time, such as The Wire, Law & Order, Criminal Minds, and The X-Files, some of them adding elements from other genres. A procedural drama TV series follows professionals and/or specialized teams who investigate a new case every episode, with some shows having overarching plots.

These shows usually have a leading pair of characters with different yet complementary personalities, becoming the heart of the show. Procedural dramas don’t forget about depth, and their main characters often struggle with trauma and other personal issues that impact their careers, as is the case with The Mentalist’s Patrick Jane. Created by Bruno Heller, The Mentalist follows Patrick Jane, a former psychic and now consultant to the California Bureau of Investigation, but his career as a psychic was a fraud.

Jane is no psychic, but he uses his highly developed observational skills to “read” people’s minds, which allowed him to pose as a psychic medium. Jane now uses those skills to solve murders, but he carries a lot of trauma that led him to change his career. The Mentalist combines a charming but broken lead with engaging cases, and luckily, Netflix has some great TV shows to watch after The Mentalist to continue on that line, but with some twists.

Will Trent is a police procedural TV series based on the book series by Karin Slaughter. Will Trent follows the title character (played by Ramón Rodríguez), a Special Agent in the Georgia Bureau of Investigation who solves the highest number of cases thanks to his incredible observation skills. Like Patrick Jane, Trent carries a lot of trauma, having been abandoned as a child and growing up in foster homes, while also facing other challenges like severe dyslexia. Both characters use unconventional methods in their investigations, with their shows balancing their darkest parts with good doses of humor.

A Man on the Inside is a comedy TV series created by Michael Schur and based on Maite Alberdi’s 2020 documentary The Mole Agent. A Man on the Inside introduces viewers to Charles (Ted Danson), a retired college engineering professor and widower who is encouraged by his daughter, Emily (Mary Elizabeth Ellis), to break out of his routine and rejoin the world.

Charles then takes a job as an investigative assistant for a private detective at Kovalenko Investigations, and so his first case is that of a missing necklace at a Pacific View Retirement Community. Unlike The Mentalist, A Man on the Inside is a more comedic show, but both are led by charming investigators who use unconventional methods and who are grieving a loved one, with their new careers helping them find a new “family.”

Dead to Me is a black comedy-crime thriller TV series created by Liz Feldman. Dead to Me follows Jen Harding (Christina Applegate) and Judy Hale (Linda Cardellini), who meet at a grief support group after Jen’s husband was killed in a hit-and-run incident and Judy claims to have lost her fiancé. In reality, Judy’s fiancé broke up with her, and she’s the hit-and-run driver. The two women form a special and deep bond, but Jen becomes more unhinged as she learns more about her husband’s death and Judy’s secrets.

Dead to Me isn’t a procedural drama, but it’s a great companion to The Mentalist thanks to their characters struggling with trauma and loss, their partner dynamics that complement each other, and how they use humor to cope with truly difficult situations.

The Following is a crime thriller TV show created by Kevin Williamson. The Following centers on Ryan Hardy (Kevin Bacon), a disgraced former FBI agent working to recapture serial killer Joe Carroll (James Purefoy) after the latter’s escape from prison. Carroll has formed a cult of fanatical killers and has his own son abducted by his people, as part of a plan to escape custody, humiliate Hardy, and reunite with his ex-wife.

The Mentalist’s Patrick Jane has a mission: capture Red John, a serial killer who murdered his family. Like Jane, The Following’s Hardy is on a mission to find Carroll, with whom he also has a connection through personal tragedy.

Marcella is a British Nordic noir detective TV series created by Hans Rosenfeldt. Marcella follows Marcella Backland (Anna Friel), a former detective at the London Metropolitan Police who returns to work to investigate three unsolved murders from 11 years earlier. However, Marcella is struggling in her personal life, as her husband of 15 years abruptly leaves her, and her two children are in boarding school.

On top of that, Marcella is dealing with dissociative blackouts that are rooted in deep trauma, tied to one specific event so traumatic that she blocked it from her memory. Marcella, like Jane, has to battle her own demons while investigating crimes and uses unconventional methods in her work, but it must be noted that Marcella is a darker show than The Mentalist.

Lupin is a French mystery thriller TV series based on the character Arssène Lupin, created by Maurice Leblanc. Lupin introduces the audience to Assane Diop (Omar Sy), a professional thief who arrives in France from Senegal hoping to build a better life for himself. When Assane was young, his father was framed for the theft of a diamond by his employer, the wealthy Hubert Pellegrini, and killed himself in prison.

Years later, Assane sets out to clear his father’s name and avenge him, and with the help of his charisma and mastery as a thief, he looks to expose Pellegrini’s crimes and bring him down. Once more, Lupin is a show with a main character carrying a lot of trauma, and just like Patrick Jane, Assane uses psychological manipulation, misdirection, and his charm to get the information he needs.

Hannibal is a psychological horror-thriller TV show based on Thomas Harris’ novels Red Dragon, Hannibal, and Hannibal Rising. Hannibal follows Will Graham (Hugh Dancy), an FBI special investigator assigned to the case of a serial killer. When the investigation turns out to have a heavy impact on Graham, his boss has him supervised by forensic psychiatrist Dr. Hannibal Lecter (Mads Mikkelsen), who is secretly a serial killer and cannibal.

Graham and Jane have similar ways of “reading” their subjects – one through observation and body language, and the other through the reconstruction of crime scenes by placing himself as the killer. Both shows have a core dynamic of opposite but complementary pairs, though Hannibal is more horror-oriented and thus is darker than The Mentalist.

Based on the character from DC Comics, Lucifer follows Lucifer Morningstar (Tom Ellis), the fallen angel-turned-lord of Hell who, bored and tired of his life in Hell, decides to abdicate his throne and move to Los Angeles, where he runs his own nightclub. After finding himself involved in a murder case, Lucifer begins working as a police consultant for the Los Angeles Police Department alongside detective Chloe Decker (Lauren German), with whom he forms a strong bond.

Like Patrick Jane, Lucifer uses his charisma and charm to get the information he needs, though he also uses his very special power to make humans tell him their deepest desires. The pairing of Lucifer and Chloe is also reminiscent of that of Jane and Teresa Lisbon, but Lucifer has fantasy elements that give the show a very interesting twist.

The Blacklist is a crime thriller TV series created by Jon Bokenkamp. The Blacklist follows Raymond Reddington (James Spader), a criminal and one of the FBI’s Most Wanted fugitives who cooperates with the FBI to capture other criminals on his “blacklist.” Reddington doesn’t have the skills that Patrick Jane has, but like him, he has his own reasons to help the FBI find other criminals, and he’s as charismatic, observant, and manipulative as Jane.

Based on John Douglas and Mark Olshaker’s 1995 true-crime book of the same name, Mindhunter follows FBI agents Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) and Bill Tench (Holt McCallany), who, along with psychologist Wendy Carr (Anna Torv), lead a research project to interview serial killers to understand their psychology and use that knowledge to solve other cases.

While Patrick Jane uses skills he has developed over the years, Mindhunter shows how those skills can be developed through deep research, and is a much deeper and more serious look into the minds of serial killers, making it a darker and more realistic complement to The Mentalist.

#3337. DHS Chief Markwayne Mullin Throws Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy Under Bus

Things got a little awkward during a press conference about the nationwide ground stop when DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin inadvertently laid blame on Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy ... before the FAA revealed they lost 12,000 flights.

It all went down Friday night ... when Mullin was asked if any cyberattack was responsible for the "extraordinary circumstances" that led to system malfunction.

Mullin said ... "What it appears to be right now, as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology and that new equipment and new technology just wasn't, it was overwhelming the older system."

As Mullin gave this response ... Duffy's system was seemingly overwhelmed too by what was said.

Hanging his head low, Duffy shook his head and at one point, may have even nudged Mullin from behind the podium. All in all ... it did not appear as if Duffy liked Mullin's response at all.

According to Duffy ... the "old legacy equipment" was to blame for the error and he warned there would be several more incidents in the future.

He said ... "This is an emergency. I want Congress to give us emergency funding. This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion."

Speaking with the press Saturday ... Duff said there's no better time than now to provide the much-needed funding ... while the FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford revealed 12,000 flights had been lost yesterday.

Saturday's press conference was a little tense too ... Bedford interrupting Duffy multiple times.

As you know ... the FAA lifted the ground stop -- that was implemented under "extraordinary circumstances" -- Friday night.

When reached for comment, the DHS and the Department of Transportation shared a press release about their joint press conference.

The AirPods Pro 3 are down to $199 from $249, saving you $50 on Apple's latest premium wireless earbuds. The Apple Magic Keyboard with Numeric Keypad is down to $109 from $129, saving you $20 on a wireless keyboard designed primarily for Mac users. It pairs wirelessly over Bluetooth and can be recharged using USB-C. For a closer look at all that it has to offer, check out PCMag's review.

The Magic Trackpad is down to $130 from $149, taking $19 off an accessory that brings the Multi-Touch gestures and Force Touch pressure sensing of a MacBook trackpad to a desktop setup, across an edge-to-edge glass surface. It connects wirelessly over Bluetooth and has a rechargeable battery that lasts about a month between charges. You can read PCMag's full review to see how it stacks up.

The Apple Pencil Pro is down to $99 from $129, saving you $30 on Apple's most feature-rich stylus. It adds squeeze and barrel-roll gestures, haptic feedback, and Find My support to Apple's stylus lineup, and it pairs and charges magnetically along the side of a compatible iPad, including the M4 iPad Air featured above. The second-generation AirTag, released in January, keeps the original's size so existing holders still fit, while a new Ultra Wideband chip extends Precision Finding range by up to 50% and a redesigned speaker plays 50% louder. Right now, its four-pack is down to $79.99 from $99.99, which works out to $20 per tag, compared with $29 for a single AirTag. Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3335. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.
